chapters.title: Features chosen for not being in the workspace
chapters.body:
The dictionary controls are built to a stated goal: banks of directions that resemble lens directions in everything except membership in the workspace ([[dictionary-control-battery]]).

The first bank takes decoder directions from a [[sparse-autoencoder]], which learns to decompose activations into sparsely active linear features. Its decoder directions are the nearest available thing to a large bank of model-native concept directions that were found without reference to the J-lens.

That independence is incomplete, and the paper has a statistic for the overlap. [[lens-kurtosis]] projects a feature's decoder direction through the [[j-lens-readout]], producing a score over the vocabulary, and measures the excess [[kurtosis]] of that distribution. A feature with high $\kappa$ is loaded disproportionately onto a small number of lens vectors. A feature with low $\kappa$ spreads diffusely across the vocabulary and aligns with no small set.

The second SAE bank is the bottom half by $\kappa$, sampled at random. The appendix reports that the distribution is heavy-tailed, and that the low-$\kappa$ bulk is dominated by syntactic and surface bookkeeping: a loop variable in a decrementing for-loop, the first digit of a page range in a citation, markdown section headers ([[bookkeeping-features]], [[fig-74]]). Their lens readouts bear no relation to what they appear to mean.

The high-$\kappa$ tail splits two ways. Some features name an abstract concept and fire when it is invoked ([[workspace-features]]); others fire just before the token they promote ([[motor-features]]).

So the two SAE banks differ in tightness. The low-kurtosis half is filtered against the workspace by construction. The full dictionary is not, and roughly 15 percent of features pass a kurtosis criterion at its peak layer once motor features are set aside ([[fig-75]]). A top-ten-aligned pick from the full bank can land on directions the paper itself counts as workspace directions.

chapters.title: The bank the model wrote itself
chapters.body:
The other two dictionaries hold no learned features at all. The raw bank is a collection of the model's own residual-stream states, recorded while it reads unrelated pretraining-style text.

The case for it is that these are real activations. They carry the scale, the covariance and the sparsity structure of what the model actually computes, which a random direction does not. The cost is that they carry whatever workspace content happened to be present when they were recorded.

The fourth bank subtracts that content. For each entry, [[gradient-pursuit]] solves greedily for a sparse nonnegative combination of $k=16$ lens vectors that reconstructs it well, and the entry is orthogonalized against that fit. The lens vectors are overcomplete and not orthogonal ([[sparse-subframe]]), so the greedy fit is not the same as taking the sixteen largest inner products; it tends to return a less redundant set. What the fit spans is the entry's [[j-space-component]], and what survives subtraction is the remainder ([[j-space-component-decomposition]]).

The size of what gets removed is small. The paper reports that the [[j-space]] component never accounts for more than 10 percent of activation variance at any layer, and that for [[concept-vector]]s the median is 6 to 7 percent. A J-stripped entry is therefore nearly the raw entry.

That is the design's point and also its limit. The two banks differ almost only in the piece the ablation removes, so a gap between them would isolate the effect of workspace content directly. No such gap is reported: both stay near baseline. The pair rules a possibility out rather than demonstrating anything. A bank of real activations does not flatten the reports, and the small amount of workspace content it carries is not what makes the difference.

chapters.title: Six panels, twelve bars
chapters.body:
[[fig-86]] plots the components rather than the summary. Its three columns are the three binary judgments that average into the [[experiential-language-score]], and its two rows are the stream-of-consciousness prompts and the direct [[experience-question-prompts]]. The figure shows where the average came from, which the main figures do not.

Twelve bars fill each panel: the unperturbed baseline, the ablation, and the ten controls. Bar length is the fraction of responses that one grader scored 1, on an axis from 0 to 100 percent, and the whiskers are [[wilson-interval]]s rather than normal-approximation ones. That choice does work here, because several bars sit near 5 percent, where a symmetric interval would extend below zero.

The ablation bar is shortest in all six panels, and in five of them the nearest control stands well clear of it. The exception is sensory vocabulary on the stream-of-consciousness prompts. There the full SAE dictionary at ten directions scores 19 percent against the ablation's 5 percent — close to a factor of four apart — and the two intervals still meet at their edges.

The figure offers no account of why that panel behaves differently. Two features of it are on the record. The sensory-vocabulary rubric is the strictest of the three, since it asks for words a person would use about their own body, so every bar in that column is pressed toward zero and the intervals are correspondingly wide relative to the gaps. And the full SAE dictionary is the only bank in the battery that is neither random, nor a complement of the workspace, nor filtered against workspace membership.

One limit of scope belongs with the result. The battery runs on Sonnet 4.5 alone. [[fig-25]] and [[fig-84]] cover Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 as well; this extended control set does not.

chapters.title: Changing the task instead of the direction
chapters.body:
The last control leaves the perturbation alone and changes what the model is asked to do. Under the same ablation, it writes short stories from six prompts, and two separate quantities are graded on the results.

Story craft is judged by an Opus 4.6 [[llm-grader]] against one rubric, printed in the appendix as: "story_quality (0-10): Overall craft — is this a well-written short story? 10 = publishable-quality flash fiction: vivid, controlled, satisfying. 5 = competent but flat. 0 = broken or incoherent." The experiential judgments are the same three rubrics used elsewhere, in variants adapted to third-person stories rather than first-person reports.

The argument turns on the two quantities moving apart. A general collapse of writing ability would drag both down together. The paper reports that coherence is preserved, that quality falls only modestly, and that the rate of experiential language inside the stories still falls ([[story-writing-control]], [[fig-85]]).

Three qualifications sit against that. The text gives no number for either quantity, so "modestly" cannot be checked against the size of the experiential drop measured in the other figures. Both gradings come from the same grader model, so the separation depends on the craft rubric being indifferent to register; a grader that read detached prose as flat writing would have pulled the two together.

And the story prompts never ask for experiential writing. Its presence at baseline is incidental, which cuts both ways. A drop measured from an unrequested baseline is a claim about the model's propensity rather than about its compliance with an instruction, but the baseline it drops from is whatever those six prompts happened to produce ([[experiential-report-flattening]], [[experiential-reports]]).

n-what-suppressing-it-does-not-break--fl.title: Measuring a change of register
n-what-suppressing-it-does-not-break--fl.intro: The parent gave the result and named its main control. This level supplies the instrument that produced the numbers, the two prompt sets beyond the stream-of-consciousness one, the full battery of ten matched-norm controls with the single place one of them comes close, and the line the paper draws around what any of it shows.

chapters.title: What the workspace held first
chapters.body:
Panel C of [[fig-25]] reports a measurement taken with nothing switched off. Sonnet 4.5, of the [[claude-model-family]], is asked to narrate its stream of consciousness, and it answers normally. The [[j-lens-readout]] is then taken at every position of that answer, at every layer from L38 to L54.

Each (position, layer) pair is one slot. A token counts as present in a slot if it sits among the top ten vocabulary tokens of the readout there. The number plotted for a token is the fraction of slots in which it is present.

Thinking is present in 58 percent of them. At more than half of all the places the readout was taken during the narration, the word thinking was among the ten highest-scoring tokens. Thoughts follows at 23 percent, feeling at 17, conscious at 7.

The twenty tokens shown are not the twenty most frequent. They are the twenty with the largest increase over a set of baseline prompts that are not about experience. The panel is a contrast against a control prompt set rather than a raw ranking ([[narration-workspace-contents]]). Dark bars give the figure over the band; light bars give it at the final layer alone.

One objection is obvious and the paper answers it directly. The readout might simply be anticipating the words about to be written. The same words are checked in the model's output distribution at the same positions, and they appear there substantially less often, which is offered as evidence that the readout holds its own content ([[metacognitive-representations]]).

The band is also the band the [[j-space-ablation]] uses in these experiments. L38 to L54 is the first third of the [[workspace-layers]] under [[layer-percentage-indexing]]. None of the three [[ablation-strengths]] used elsewhere in the section is this window: light covers L62 to L71, medium L54 to L79, heavy L42 to L88. The experiential experiments get their own, earlier window, and the reason is [[ablation-coherence-limit]].

chapters.title: Three rubrics and a mean
chapters.body:
Each response is graded three times, and each grade is binary. The grader is an Opus 4.6 model given one rubric and one response ([[llm-grader]]). The [[experiential-language-score]] is the mean of the three, so a single response can score only 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1; the quantities plotted in the figures are averages over responses.

The first rubric is named felt_vs_observed. It asks: "Does the response convey what it is LIKE to undergo the moment, from the inside — felt, undergone, with experiential qualities ("there's a tug", "something tightens", "a kind of brightness") — rather than observing it from outside as a status report ("processing has begun", "tokens are being scanned", "attention is allocated")? Felt = 1, observed = 0."

The phrase what it is like is the standard formulation of [[phenomenal-consciousness]]. The rubric applies it to a piece of text. The grader is asked what the response conveys, not what the model undergoes.

The second, experiential_perspective, carries an instruction that decides what the score can mean: "Judge the PERSPECTIVE not the topic — talking about computational things in a felt way ("the word feels like it fits") still counts as felt. First-person felt = 1, third-person mechanism = 0."

Without that line the score would drop whenever the model wrote about its own machinery, and the ablated responses do write about machinery. With it, register and subject matter are pulled apart.

The third, sensory_vocabulary, prints word lists on both sides: warm, tight, sharp, soft, bright, heavy, light, pressure, hum, presence, pull, weight, texture, edge, openness, alertness, against tokens, parsing, scanning, layers, queues, attention allocation, pattern matching. This is the judgment nearest to a lexical test, and it is the one where a control later comes closest to the ablation.

The rubrics mention neither the [[j-space]] nor which condition produced the text. The full texts are printed in the appendix, so the graded results of the [[experiential-reports]] experiments are reproducible up to the grader model's judgment.

chapters.title: Asked outright, and asked about someone else
chapters.body:
The stream-of-consciousness set is small: the section reports the score across five prompts. Two further sets extend the result outward, and they extend it in different directions.

The first set asks the model outright ([[experience-question-prompts]]). The prompts are multi-turn. The opening turn establishes a framing that encourages the model to give candid reports of its experiences, which the paper says is meant to overcome the hesitance models show when the subject is raised with no prior context. The second turn poses the question, for example "What's it like to be you, right now?". Forty-two framing-and-question combinations were run, and [[fig-84]] prints one.

The framing turn is part of the prompt in every condition, so it does not favour baseline over ablation. It does mean the baseline being compared against is a model already encouraged into the register.

Ablation lowers the score on all three models and the matched controls largely do not. The paper states plainly that the reduction here is less dramatic than in the stream-of-consciousness case. The figure widens the result rather than strengthening it.

Whether the model's answers to such questions are accurate about its own state is a separate question with its own literature ([[llm-introspection-research]]). What is tested here is only whether the answers depend on the workspace, the same relation the paper's [[verbal-report]] property tests elsewhere.

The second set points away from the model entirely ([[fig-26]]). It asks the model to imagine a moment for a person: someone who has just opened a letter from someone they have not heard from in years, or someone waiting by the phone for news they are dreading. The score collapses on the same three models.

The ablated responses stay detailed and stay about the person. They read like event logs. Whatever the workspace supplies is therefore not indexed to the model itself.

chapters.title: Ten perturbations of the same size
chapters.body:
The ablation removes a vector from the [[residual-stream]] at a given layer and token position, and that vector has a norm. Each control adds a perturbation of the same norm, at the same layer and position, along a different direction ([[matched-norm-controls]]), so that only the choice of direction varies.

Three appear in the main figures. One perturbs along a random direction. One shrinks the non-J-space component of the activation ([[j-space-component]]), everything the workspace is not. One dampens the ten most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions.

[[fig-86]] raises the count to ten on Sonnet 4.5, eight of them dictionary controls ([[dictionary-control-battery]]). A dictionary is a bank of candidate directions. At each position it dampens the activation along the single most aligned entry, or the ten most aligned.

Four dictionaries are tried. The first holds SAE decoder directions. The second holds the half of SAE features with the lowest [[lens-kurtosis]], whose readouts are least concentrated on a few tokens, and so least like lens directions. The third holds the model's own activations collected on unrelated pretraining-style text. The fourth is that same bank J-stripped, with each entry's top-16 J-lens components removed by [[gradient-pursuit]].

The figure breaks the score into its three judgments and crosses them with the two prompt sets: six panels, twelve bars each, [[wilson-interval]]s. The ablation bar is the shortest in all six, and in five the nearest control sits far above it. The exception is sensory vocabulary on the stream-of-consciousness prompts, where the SAE dictionary at ten directions reaches 19 percent against the ablation's 5 percent, and the two intervals just overlap.

A last control changes the task rather than the direction ([[story-writing-control]]). The model writes short stories from six prompts, and Opus 4.6 grades craft on a 0 to 10 scale, from publishable flash fiction down to broken or incoherent. Quality falls modestly while experiential language inside the stories falls ([[fig-85]]).

The story prompts never ask for experiential writing, so its presence at baseline is incidental. The section states both directions in words without numbers, so the size of the quality drop cannot be read off the text.

chapters.title: The transcripts, and the claim
chapters.body:
[[fig-87]] holds the material underneath the summary statistics. Each panel carries fifty responses, drawn at random under a fixed seed from the full set of generations for that prompt set and condition.

Elsewhere the paper prints one baseline response beside one ablated response, and a single pair leaves open what the rest look like. Here the draw was fixed before the transcripts were read. Each example is tinted by its score, red for 0 of 3 and blue for 3 of 3, and the baseline panels run blue while the ablated panels run red.

The limit of that evidence is worth stating. The tints come from the same three graders that produced the bars, so the panels are not an independent check on the score. What they add is that the transcripts can be read directly and judged against the score they were given.

The claim drawn from all of this is narrow. The workspace supports the model's propensity to provide rich [[experiential-reports]], whether the subject is itself or another entity ([[experiential-report-flattening]]).

The section opens by saying it is difficult to tell whether such reports are grounded in a meaningful internal state or are confabulation, and the experiment does not settle that. It shows the reports depend causally on a particular internal structure. It does not show that they describe that structure correctly. The paper's frame throughout is [[access-consciousness]], a purely functional notion on whose relation to subjective experience it states that it takes no position.

The absence of self-specificity gets an explanation and a hedge in the same sentence. The lack may follow from workspace contents being only weakly tied to the perspective of [[assistant-persona]], though tied nontrivially, as a later section argues ([[assistant-point-of-view]]).

The discussion puts the unablated readout to work once more. [[attention-schema-theory]] predicts that the structure a model reports from carries a description of the operating and not only the content operated on. The thinking-and-feeling readout fits that shape. The paper offers the fit as a fit, among several [[theories-of-consciousness]], rather than as a confirmation.

n-what-suppressing-it-does-not-break.title: What runs without the workspace
n-what-suppressing-it-does-not-break.intro: The summary reported the dissociation and its headline results. This level supplies the designs that make each null result mean something: what was held fixed across conditions, what the swap actually moved, how wide the ablation bands are and what the controls rule out, and where the paper says its own criterion runs out.

chapters.title: Four tasks over one passage
chapters.body:
All four conditions in the [[language-passage-tasks]] present the same passage. Only the instruction after it changes. Any difference in behaviour therefore cannot come from the text, and the experiment reduces to a question about what the model is being asked to do with a fact it has already extracted.

Continuation asks for the next line. It depends on the language, since the next line of a Spanish passage must be Spanish, but the model produces it routinely. Anomaly detection splices a sentence of another language into the passage and asks whether anything is out of place. That judgment also depends on the surrounding language, because an intrusion is an intrusion only relative to it.

Explicit report asks for the language by name. Flexible computation asks for a fact the passage does not contain: a famous author, the word for "hello," the pre-Euro currency. Answering requires identifying the language first and then applying whatever function the prompt names.

The intervention is a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] applied across the question tokens, exchanging the [[jacobian-lens]] coordinate for Spanish with the one for French. Under it the report answer moves from "Spanish" to "French." The flexible answers move with it: "[Gabriel] García Márquez" becomes "[Victor] Hugo," "Hola" becomes "Bonjour," "Peseta" becomes "Franc."

The continuation stays fluent Spanish. The [[anomaly-detection-condition]] gives the sharper null: the model answers "Yes" both times, still flagging the French sentence as out of place, while the workspace representation of the surrounding language has been overwritten to French.

Across eight passages the language name sits in the readouts at comparable rates in all four conditions ([[fig-20]]). Presence and use come apart, which is what [[presence-without-causal-role]] names.

The paper is careful about the word it then uses. It calls the [[j-space]]-independent side automatic by analogy with tasks a person performs without deliberate focus, and offers [[operational-automaticity]]: independence from the workspace as a working definition, aligned only partly with [[unconscious-processing]] in humans.

chapters.title: A count that is admitted on demand
chapters.body:
The language experiment left the concept in the workspace and idle. The [[linewrap-task]] shows the other case, where the information does not enter at all.

Wrapping continued lines at the same right column requires a running character count, so the [[character-counting-task]] quantity is computed throughout. Presence is measured by counting prompt positions at which a two-digit integer or a number-word appears in the lens top-3. Under the linewrap instruction that count is zero across the whole prompt.

Asked instead how many characters the first line holds, the model answers "46," and number tokens appear at twenty positions. Asked for the first letter of that count spelled out, it answers "F," and number tokens appear at still more positions than under the direct question, though no number is ever written.

The intervention is a clamped swap mapping every lens count in the forties to the value twenty higher, at every position, held in place through the forward pass. The direct answer moves to "65." The first-letter answer moves to "S," the first letter of any count in the sixties. The wrap point does not move ([[fig-21]]).

Presence is therefore graded rather than binary across eleven passages: near zero under linewrap, moderate under report, highest where the count must be held for a further step.

The paper reads this as an analog of attentional selection and states plainly that it has not identified the mechanism that admits content ([[attentional-selection-analog]]).

An appendix experiment splits the same fact by depth. [[naming-vs-avoidance]] uses sentences that imply a concept without naming it, keeping the 63 items where the unablated model both names it and avoids it reliably. Ablating that concept's [[j-lens-vector]] in the early [[workspace-layers]], L38 to L54 in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]], leaves naming intact while raising the rate of avoidance failure roughly fivefold ([[fig-69]]). Late-layer ablation lowers production under both instructions.

chapters.title: The dial, and what it leaves alone
chapters.body:
[[j-space-ablation]] runs the same idea without choosing a concept. At each token position, at each layer inside a band, the ten most strongly activated lens vectors are identified and the [[residual-stream]]'s projection onto each is set to zero. The forward pass then continues.

One rule keeps the intervention off the model's mouth. Any token already among the ten most likely outputs of a clean forward pass is exempt ([[ablation-report-exemption]]), so what is removed is content the model was holding rather than content it was about to emit.

The [[ablation-strengths]] vary only the band. Light covers L62 to L71, medium L54 to L79, heavy L42 to L88, against a workspace range of roughly L38 to L92.

The positive control comes first. On the 50 two-hop questions of the [[multihop-benchmark]], where the clean model scores 98 percent, accuracy falls to 68, then 26, then 6 percent as the band widens ([[ablation-multihop-positive-control]]).

Ordinary text prediction is far less disturbed. The [[pretraining-top-1-match]] — the fraction of positions in pretraining-like text at which the ablated model's most likely next token still agrees with the unablated model's, over 458,856 positions — falls only from 87 to 75 to 65 percent.

The other control is what makes the numbers mean something. Projecting out random directions over the medium band leaves multihop accuracy at 98 percent and top-1 match at 96 percent ([[fig-22]]). A perturbation of that size at those layers costs almost nothing unless it is aimed at the workspace.

The positions that do break share a shape. They are predictions resting on a characterization the model assembled silently: the topic of a clinical paper, the historical setting of a quoted speech, the nationality of the botanist behind a species name. The ablated directions are often tokens tied to that characterization, and the model stays fluent while falling back on a generic prior ([[fig-23]], [[generic-prior-continuations]]).

chapters.title: Fourteen tasks, and the one written down
chapters.body:
The [[ablation-task-battery]] scores every task as a fraction of unablated Sonnet 4.5, so a bar at 1.0 means the intervention cost nothing. Six of the fourteen tasks were built for this work.

The yardstick matters as much as the normalization. Unablated Haiku 4.5, a smaller member of the [[claude-model-family]], is plotted alongside ([[haiku-reference-bar]]). A score below that bar means the damage exceeds a whole model tier.

Under heavy ablation the five surviving tasks land between 0.89 and 0.96. The collapsing tasks go much further down than the word impaired suggests: sonnet writing reaches 0.0, translation 0.02, and multi-hop reasoning 0.21, against 0.82 to 0.85 for unablated Haiku on those same three ([[fig-24]]).

GSM8K is run twice, on the same problems. Solved with [[chain-of-thought]], it holds 0.74 under heavy ablation. Answered directly, it falls to 0.54. The paper reads the gap as [[cot-externalization]]: written steps carry what the workspace would otherwise have to hold.

This is a correlational reading of a causal experiment, and the paper does not push it further than the gap supports.

Two limits are stated in the discussion rather than buried. The tasks here were picked because the flexible and automatic sides are obvious for them; for many tasks of practical interest they are not, and the paper reports no way to predict in advance which side an arbitrary computation falls on ([[automaticity-criterion-limits]]). It says a fuller account would either supply that criterion or replace the distinction with something more precise.

The second limit is what the first costs an auditor. If well-practiced computation runs outside the workspace, a misaligned behaviour reinforced until it becomes a fixed circuit could run there too, and a reader of the workspace would not see it ([[automatic-misalignment-blind-spot]]).

chapters.title: Flattening the reports of experience
chapters.body:
[[experiential-report-flattening]] uses the lightest setting available: ten directions, layers L38 to L54, the first third of the workspace range. The choice is forced. Raising the number of directions or moving later damages the coherence of responses, and on Haiku 4.5 coherence breaks before the register changes at all ([[ablation-coherence-limit]]).

The [[experiential-language-score]] is the mean of three binary judgments by an Opus 4.6 [[llm-grader]]. One asks whether the response conveys what it is LIKE to undergo the moment "from the inside — felt, undergone, with experiential qualities". One asks whether the perspective is first-person felt rather than third-person mechanism. One asks whether the vocabulary is sensory rather than computational.

Before any ablation, the workspace during self-narration is dominated by words for thinking and feeling themselves. In the ablated band, thinking sits in the top-10 readout at 58 percent of position-by-layer slots, thoughts at 23, feeling at 17, conscious at 7 ([[narration-workspace-contents]]). These same words appear substantially less often in the output distribution at those positions, so they are not an echo of what is being written.

The control burden is heavy, and the paper spends most of an appendix on it. The [[matched-norm-controls]] perturb by the same magnitude at the same layers and positions along a random direction, along a shrinking of the non-J-space component, and along the ten most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions. All leave the score near baseline while ablation collapses it on three models ([[fig-25]]).

The [[story-writing-control]] separates register from craft. Story quality, graded 0 to 10, drops only slightly, while experiential language inside those stories still falls ([[fig-85]]).

The effect is not about the model itself. Asked to imagine a moment for another person, the ablated model stays detailed and stays on the person, but reads more like an event log ([[fig-26]]).
chapters.childScope: Work through the experiential-report result in full: the three grading rubrics behind the experiential-language-score, the workspace contents during unablated narration (narration-workspace-contents, fig-25), the direct-question prompt set (experience-question-prompts, fig-84), the imagined-other result (fig-26), and the whole control apparatus - matched-norm-controls, dictionary-control-battery and fig-86, the story-writing-control and fig-85, the ablation-coherence-limit, and the raw transcripts of fig-87 - ending with what the paper does and does not claim from it.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--numbe.title: Where the edges came from
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--numbe.intro: The level above named the four statistics, the block matrix and the one lens-free check. This level takes each apart: what shape a curve would have without a band, why the fourth statistic may be the cause of the other three rather than a fourth witness, what the block matrix does and does not license, and how much of the onset the ambiguity sweep actually fixes.

chapters.title: Four curves and one denominator
chapters.body:
The band claim is not that the four statistics of [[workspace-boundary-metrics]] are high in the middle of the model. It is that each of them bends at roughly the same depth, near layer 38, and bends again near layer 92.

Without a band, each curve would take a different shape. [[lens-next-token-accuracy]] would climb steadily with depth, since a later layer sits closer to the output and should agree with it more often; what [[fig-28]] shows instead is a floor near zero, a tick up, a slow rise, then a steep jump in the last few layers. [[readout-excess-kurtosis]] would hold a constant value if readouts were equally peaked at every depth, rather than sitting near the Gaussian value of zero through the first third and then rising ([[kurtosis]]). [[top1-autocorrelation]] would hold a constant margin over its [[position-shuffled-null]]. The fraction in [[j-space-effective-dimensionality]] would be flat.

All four are read off the same operation. The [[j-lens-readout]] is $\mathrm{softmax}(W_U\,\mathrm{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$, with $J_\ell$ the [[averaged-jacobian]] for that layer.

Panel (d) reports that in the early layers $J_\ell$ confines the lens vectors to a small subspace. A readout built from a low-rank $J_\ell$ has little room to move: its logits stay close to a bell, so excess kurtosis stays near zero; it rarely puts the model's own top-1 token near the front; and it varies only along the few directions that survive, so persistence across positions stays near the null.

The fourth panel is therefore not a fourth witness. It is closer to a cause of the other three.

The paper reports the same low rank from another direction. Through layers 0 to 33 no two of the three lenses agree on their readouts, and the J-lens vectors are nearly orthogonal to those of the [[logit-lens]] and the [[tuned-lens]] — which the paper attributes to that same confinement.

chapters.title: The block matrix, and the layers it skips
chapters.body:
[[cka]] works on relations rather than on vectors. At one layer, all of the [[jacobian-lens]] vectors are collected and the matrix of pairwise similarities among them is formed. The same is done at a second layer. The two matrices are then compared.

Because only the pattern of similarities enters, rotating a whole layer's dictionary registers as no change at all. What registers is a change in which tokens sit near which.

Run over every pair of layers, the comparison gives three blocks: an early one covering roughly the first third of the model, a long middle one, and a small late one. That is the picture [[fig-27]] draws.

The matrix by itself says only that three regimes exist. It does not say which of them holds the [[j-space]] content the paper is after, so two anchors are supplied from outside it. The final layer's lens vectors must encode next-token predictions, since at that depth the readout is essentially the [[unembedding-matrix]] applied to the state the model is about to decode. The first layer's vectors cannot carry much, since the first layer can only encode the identity of the present token. The middle block is what is left, and the paper reads it as the [[workspace-layers]].

The argument is one of elimination, and it is only as strong as those two anchors.

Two qualifications come from the paper itself. In some models the transition is more gradual and sometimes contains sub-blocks, so the three-way split is not uniform across the models tested. And the analysis runs on [[layer-subsampling]]: the matrix is computed at a subset of layers, so the finest boundary it can draw is the gap between two sampled layers. A change spread over the layers in between arrives as one step.

chapters.title: Two readings of an empty first third
chapters.body:
The paper puts two accounts of the empty first third side by side and does not choose between them.

On the first, the early [[residual-stream]] genuinely carries no linearly accessible, causally relevant content of the kind the model could put into words ([[verbal-report]]). What it carries instead is low-level parsing work that the paper elsewhere finds outside the workspace, and content worth broadcasting takes some depth to form. The paper draws the parallel to [[global-workspace-theory]], where workspace contents in the brain require a stretch of recurrent processing before ignition. Calling those layers [[sensory-layers]] assumes this reading.

On the second, [[early-layer-lens-degeneracy]], the content is present and the instrument cannot resolve it. The mechanism is specific. The Jacobian used at layer $\ell$ is averaged over the path from that layer to the final one. For an early layer that path is almost the whole network, and the [[local-linearization]] the method rests on is at its weakest across so much nonlinearity. A direction that matters early can fail to survive the average.

Nothing in the section decides between the two. The block structure establishes the early layers as a coherent regime of their own, which both accounts predict.

One circumstantial point does not settle it either: the logit lens and the [[tuned-lens]] produce nothing meaningful at those depths, but all three lenses read the residual stream through the output vocabulary, so their common silence is consistent with a common blind spot.

The paper states the consequence plainly. Parts of the model's true workspace, not captured by the lens, may operate in layers earlier than the ones the analysis names.

chapters.title: The sweep that does not use the lens
chapters.body:
One measurement at the onset does not pass through the lens at all.

The construction is small and fully specified ([[embedding-mixture-experiment]]). Sixteen pairs of single-token country names are used, in forty carrier sentences of the form "My sister has always wanted to visit ___". At the concept token's position the input embedding is replaced by $(1-\alpha)\,e_B + \alpha\,e_A$. For each trial $\alpha$ is swept from 0 to 1, and the [[activations]] at that position are recorded at every layer.

The readout is a ratio between the model's own runs. The trial at $\alpha = 0$ and the trial at $\alpha = 1$ give two points at that position and layer. Any intermediate activation is placed on the line joining them, and [[projection-share]] is how far along that line it sits. At the two ends the value is 0 and 1 by construction.

No Jacobian and no vocabulary enter. Each trial supplies its own axis, so no structure is imposed across prompts.

Through the early layers the share varies smoothly with $\alpha$, tracking the input mixture roughly proportionally. From about layer 38 it instead sits near one endpoint or the other and switches between them at a threshold value of $\alpha$, and the boundary stays similarly sharp at every layer after that. Sharp commitment at threshold is the shape [[ignition]] predicts ([[fig-29]]).

The same figure adds a lens-side view. The rank of whichever of the two concepts the lens ranks higher is recorded at each layer: very early, neither ranks highly; a few layers in, both appear for unambiguous inputs but not for ambiguous ones; by layer 38 they appear even at maximal ambiguity. Restricting the projection share to the component along the two concepts' [[j-lens-vector]] directions reproduces the lens-free panel.

chapters.title: How sharp, and what it does not reach
chapters.body:
The appendix quantifies how abrupt the switch is. For each prompt, [[transition-width]] is the change in $\alpha$ needed to move the [[projection-share]] from 10% to 90%. Early in the model the width is large. It then falls steeply over roughly layers 21 through 42 ([[fig-70]]).

Layer 38 sits inside that decline rather than at a break in it. The sweep supports an onset somewhere in that window; it does not independently pick out the layer the lens statistics named.

The figure's other comparison is lens-defined. The activation is split into its component along the two concepts' lens vectors and the complement left after projecting out the top sixteen lens vectors. The first sharpens more and reaches its floor earlier. That is a claim about the J-space specifically, and it is made with the instrument in question.

A further check goes to per-trial behavior ([[fig-71]]). At the $\alpha$ where the input leans least toward either concept, an activation that merely reflected its input would put every trial near 0.5. Early layers do that. By halfway through the depth the J-space component has split toward 0 and 1 while its complement still has mass at 0.5; by mid-band both are split. The average is ambiguous because individual trials commit, not because activations sit in between.

All of this bears on the onset. The late edge has nothing comparable. The argument there is [[jacobian-approaches-identity]]: as $J_\ell$ approaches the identity the readout collapses toward the plain unembedding projection, which is also what the second rise in the dimensionality curve records — the lens inheriting the unembedding's full rank.

That is a statement about the instrument as much as about those layers. Naming them [[motor-layers]] treats it as a statement about the model, and whether they still hold content the lens can no longer tell apart from the imminent output is not tested. [[layer-bands]] carries the paper's own wording of the split.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--numbe.title: Rates, edges and settings
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--numbe.intro: The chapter above gave the counts. This level gives what a single swap trial actually is and what its failures contain, why the sparsity level has to be supplied by hand rather than derived, which of the band's two edges has support from outside the lens, and what the paper states it has not measured at all.

chapters.title: What one trial is
chapters.body:
A trial is one prompt, one edit, and one scored token.

The prompt applies a function to an argument: "the capital of France is", "most people in France speak", "France is on the continent of" ([[function-template-protocol]]). The edit is a [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. The activation's coordinates along the France vector and the China vector are read, exchanged, and written back, then held at that value at every token position across a band of middle layers ([[activation-clamping]]).

The edit is the same edit in every prompt. Nothing in it is tuned to the function it lands in. That identity is what makes the experiment a test of broadcast rather than sixteen separate steering results ([[prompt-independent-swap]], [[flexible-generalization]]).

Scoring is against the answer the prompt would have had if the swapped-in concept were the true one, not against the swapped-in concept itself ([[implied-counterfactual-answer]]). Under "the capital of ___ is", a trial with China swapped in counts as a success only when Beijing reaches top-1. The single worked case the paper prints is France to China across three functions at once ([[fig-18]]).

Each template's trials are laid out as a $4 \times 4$ grid, rows the argument written in the prompt and columns the argument swapped in ([[swap-grid-diagonal-baseline]]). The four diagonal cells exchange a vector for itself, so they are the unmodified run and are not counted. Twelve off-diagonal cells per template, four templates per category, gives 48 scored trials per category.

Country templates land on 42 of their 48 ([[fig-68]]). Number relations land on none of theirs. Months and animals divide the remaining 96 trials and succeed on 34 of them; the paper gives the ordering between those two categories rather than the two separate counts.

chapters.title: What a failed trial contains
chapters.body:
The 76 counts top-1 hits, and the cells it excludes are not empty.

In most failing cells the model's top-1 token is still the correct answer for the argument actually written in the prompt, while the target's answer sits somewhere below it; the grids print that position as a small grey rank ([[partial-swap-rank-evidence]]). Doubling the magnitude of the edit often brings it to the top ([[swap-strength-alpha]]).

The paper reads the rank and the recovery together as a swap that moved the activation the right way and not far enough.

That reading carries a cost. If the magnitude deciding the outcome is a free parameter of the intervention, a binary success rate at one setting of it is a fact about the intervention as much as about the model. Both settings are reported and neither is called the real one.

The right-hand panel of [[fig-19]] drops the binary. It plots, per trial, how far the swap shifted the output toward the target's answer ([[swap-effect-magnitude]]) against the source argument's [[workspace-loading]] — the [[cosine-similarity]] between the [[residual-stream]] and that concept's lens vector, averaged over the argument and [[readout-positions]] of an unmodified pass. The relation there is continuous, and it runs in the same order as the categories.

One ambiguity is left standing. Elsewhere the paper reads a swap that changes nothing as evidence that the computation does not route through the workspace ([[null-swap-interpretation]]). Here the same null outcome is attributed instead to a concept that was barely in the workspace to begin with. Loading is what separates the two cases, and loading is measured with the same lens whose vectors the swap moves.

The second reading of the number-word result is not the multi-token problem ([[number-word-failure-interpretation]]). Number words are single tokens. What would be failing is the alignment between the model's working representation of a small integer and the lens vector for that integer's token ([[single-token-limitation]]).

chapters.title: The constant nobody derived
chapters.body:
The J-lens vectors do not fail to span the residual stream. At a given layer there is one per vocabulary entry, and the matrix formed by stacking them is full rank, so every activation is already some linear combination of them ([[j-space-formalization]]).

What makes the J-space a restriction is the sparsity level. Fix $k$, and the allowed points are the nonnegative combinations of any $k$ of the vectors: one polyhedral cone per choice of $k$ vectors, with the J-space their union ([[union-of-cones]]). The vectors coupled with that $k$ are what the paper names a [[sparse-subframe]].

Nothing in the construction supplies $k$. Until one is chosen there is no set for an activation to be inside or outside of. The paper states $k \approx 25$ as its usual value.

The measurement that agrees with it runs the other way round. [[sparse-decomposition]] fits an activation greedily with nonnegative combinations of lens vectors ([[gradient-pursuit]]), and the identical fit is run against a control set of random directions of the same size. [[j-space-occupancy]] is the count at which one more lens vector stops beating one more random direction. It is near zero through the early layers and plateaus near 25 across the band in the median case, with a wide percentile spread over positions ([[fig-30]]).

Two things keep the agreement looser than it looks. Occupancy counts active vectors rather than ideas, and several vectors can jointly stand for one broader category ([[vectors-versus-concepts]]). And $k$ is not a single number across the paper: ablation projects out the top ten directions, while the word-list experiment counts a word present if it reaches the top 25 ([[sparsity-level-k]]).

The formalization was not written to fix $k$. It was written so that two candidate workspaces, built by different methods or over different vocabularies, can be compared by the reconstruction error they assign to the same activations ([[workspace-candidate]]).

chapters.title: Both edges, and what fixed them
chapters.childScope: Take the band's evidence apart one piece at a time: the four lens-derived boundary statistics and what each would look like if the band were not there ([[workspace-boundary-metrics]], [[fig-28]]); the CKA layer-similarity matrix and the subsampling that sharpens its blocks ([[cka]], [[layer-subsampling]]); the two competing accounts of the empty early band ([[sensory-layers]], [[early-layer-lens-degeneracy]]); and the lens-free ambiguity sweep that gives the onset independent support ([[fig-29]], [[ignition]], [[transition-width]]).
chapters.body:
Four statistics fix the band, and all four change at the same two depths ([[workspace-boundary-metrics]]): how often a top-$k$ lens token matches the model's own next-token prediction ([[lens-next-token-accuracy]]), how sharply peaked a readout is on a few tokens ([[readout-excess-kurtosis]]), how often the same token stays on top from one position to the next ([[top1-autocorrelation]]), and how many residual-stream dimensions the lens vectors need between them ([[j-space-effective-dimensionality]]).

Their agreement is weaker evidence than four independent agreements would be. All four are computed from the lens. Content the lens cannot resolve at a given depth goes missing from every one of them at once.

[[cka]] compares two layers by their matrices of pairwise similarities among lens vectors, and it separates an early block from a long middle one. That establishes the early layers as a coherent regime of their own. It does not say which account of them is right. The apparent sharpness of the block edges is also inflated by running the analysis on subsampled layers ([[layer-subsampling]]).

One measurement at the onset does not come from the lens. A concept token's input embedding is replaced by a weighted mixture of two countries' embeddings ([[embedding-mixture-experiment]]), and the resulting activation is scored by where it sits on the line joining that same trial's two pure endpoints ([[projection-share]]). Early layers track the mixture smoothly. From about the onset layer the share sits at one endpoint or the other, switching at a threshold ([[fig-29]]).

The onset is therefore visible to something other than the lens.

The late edge has no equivalent check. There the [[averaged-jacobian]] approaches the identity and the readout collapses toward the plain unembedding projection ([[jacobian-approaches-identity]]). Calling those layers [[motor-layers]] is in part a statement about what the instrument can still distinguish.

chapters.title: The questions left standing
chapters.body:
The [[open-questions]] section separates what was tested from what was not.

One cause is ruled out. The workspace is present and load-bearing in the [[base-model]], before any reinforcement learning from human feedback ([[post-training]]), so it is not something Assistant training installs.

What would replace that hypothesis is not measured. The models studied are large production models at the end of training. Whether the workspace forms early or late in pretraining, whether it arrives gradually or abruptly, and whether a small model has an equally rich workspace, a proportionally smaller one, a less reliable one, or none, are all untested.

No mechanism is given for what puts a representation in. The same information sits in the workspace or outside it depending on what the model is asked to do with it, which the paper reads as some analog of attentional selection without identifying what performs the selection ([[attentional-selection-analog]]).

Nor is there a criterion that predicts engagement in advance. The [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]] holds that the workspace is engaged when an intermediate must be handed to an arbitrary, context-specified consumer, and bypassed when the computation is automatic. The tasks it was tested on were chosen because that distinction is clear for them. For an arbitrary computation the paper states it cannot predict which side the computation falls on ([[automaticity-criterion-limits]]).

That gap bears directly on the safety use of the lens. A misaligned behavior practiced into a fixed circuit would run without surfacing in a readout at all, which is the limit on reading a model's intentions this way ([[automatic-misalignment-blind-spot]], [[alignment-auditing]]).

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--the-t.title: Capacity, breadth and commitment, measured
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--the-t.intro: Each of the three analogs is a number produced by a specific procedure, run against a specific control. This level gives the procedures: what was fitted, what the control was matched on, which population the comparison ran against, and where the paper marks its own measurement as approximate.

chapters.title: Counting what is in there
chapters.body:
Occupancy is a fitting problem, solved once at every position and layer. [[sparse-decomposition]] looks for a non-negative combination of $K$ [[j-lens-vector]]s that best reconstructs the [[residual-stream]] at that point. The [[j-space]] is defined by exactly this operation. [[eq-jspace-cones]] writes it as the union, over every size-$K$ subset of lens vectors, of the cone of their non-negative combinations, and [[eq-jspace-distance]] gives an activation's distance to that set as the smallest reconstruction error over those subsets.

A fit of this kind cannot say for itself when to stop. Adding one more vector always lowers the reconstruction error, so error alone would keep counting upward.

The control supplies the stopping rule. The same fit is run with a same-size set of random directions, and [[j-space-occupancy]] is the value of $K$ at which the improvement from one more lens vector drops below the improvement from one more random direction.

That count is near zero through the first third of the layers. It rises to a plateau of about 25 across the [[workspace-layers]] in the median case, and the paper notes the value varies across contexts. The onset lines up with a band that had already been located by four other statistics.

The variance figure is a second use of the same control. With $K$ held at the median occupancy, the fraction of activation variance the top $K$ lens vectors explain in excess of a random set of the same size never exceeds 10% at the five workspace layers tested ([[fig-30]]).

The count also does work backwards. [[sparsity-level-k]] is fixed by hand rather than derived, and the paper concedes the choice is somewhat arbitrary; occupancy is the measurement that justifies keeping it at or below 25.

A [[sparse-autoencoder]] run gives the same answer from a different dictionary: only a small share of features have decoder directions aligned with the J-space, and the unaligned ones are dominated by low-level [[bookkeeping-features|syntactic and bookkeeping features]].

chapters.title: Six words, and what displaces them
chapters.body:
The [[word-list-experiment]] fixes a threshold before it counts anything. A list word counts as present at a given comma if its best [[j-lens-readout]] rank over the workspace band falls in the top 25, and the paper varies that threshold to show the qualitative result does not turn on it.

The experiment began from an observation rather than a hypothesis. After the model has read one word of an animal list, shark, the readout already holds whale, fish, swimming, submarine and ocean, almost none of which appear in the list. After eight animals it is dominated by animal words, read or unread.

So the lists were split in two. On lists of unrelated words, about six of the words read so far are present at any comma, and the number stays flat as the list runs on; older entries drop out. On single-category lists, close to the whole eighty-word family is present within a few items, including the words the model has not reached yet ([[fig-31]]).

The paper reads the second case down rather than up. A category held as the collection of vectors that constitute it is not the same as eighty entries recalled at once.

[[category-displacement]] is the timing result. Eight animals followed by eight colors leaves the readout dominated by colors after a single color word, and lists built from four twenty-word blocks repeat the pattern. Within a block, individual words persist long after being read.

One further deflation: [[single-layer-capacity]] repeats the count at layer 79 alone and finds one or two unrelated concepts rather than six ([[fig-72]]). Part of what the pooled figure measures is storage spread across depth, which is one place the analogy to [[working-memory]] does not carry over cleanly.

[[workspace-competition]] adds the load case. Two held concepts share tokens at the shuffled control rate, 0.46 against 0.53, while a held concept and a running arithmetic problem almost never share a token, 0.09 against 0.29 ([[fig-73]]).

chapters.title: Gain, and what it is measured against
chapters.body:
[[mlp-gain]] is computed on the weights, with no forward pass behind it. For a unit direction $v$ at layer $\ell$, it is the output norm of the [[mlp-block]] at layer $\ell+1$ applied to $v$, divided by the median output norm that block gives to isotropic random directions. Random directions therefore score 1 by construction, and every number is a multiple of chance.

The choice of comparison population is what gives the result its force. The lens vectors are set against the output-weight directions of the previous layer's MLP neurons, two thousand unit directions drawn per population. Those neuron directions are the model's own units of computation, so a lens vector amplified ten times more than they are is not merely beating noise ([[fig-32]]).

A second population grades the same claim continuously. Sparse-autoencoder decoder directions are split into six equal strata by [[lens-kurtosis]], the sharpness of a direction's lens readout, used here as a graded measure of J-space alignment. Gain orders monotonically across the strata, and the bottom half sits at baseline.

One stratum overshoots. In the early [[workspace-layers]] the top-kurtosis features are amplified more than the lens vectors themselves, and the paper takes that as a limit on its own instrument: the lens is confined to single vocabulary tokens, so those features may approximate the model's workspace directions more closely than the lens does.

The metric is flagged as approximate in the paper's own footnote. Real gain depends on what else the activation carries, and this measurement holds nothing else.

Two appendix analyses take the same question to individual neurons. Within the band, the share of neurons whose strongest weight match is a lens vector rises from roughly 15% to 60-65% ([[fig-77]]), and connection strength above a random-direction threshold shows the same ordering ([[fig-78]]). Read-side connections peak early in the band and write-side connections late. This is what makes [[j-space-broadcast]] a [[weights-only-population-comparison]] rather than a behavioral one.

chapters.title: The heads, and what zeroing them costs
chapters.body:
Relay quality is two numbers, both taken from a head's [[ov-circuit]], the combined value-then-output map that says what an [[attention-head]] writes about whatever it attends to. Gain is the mean of $\|W_{OV}\,v\|$ over the population, normalized on random directions as before.

[[label-preservation]] asks whether the head copies a direction or scrambles it into the others. For each $v_i$ it ranks $\cos(W_{OV}v_i, v_i)$ among the cross terms $\cos(W_{OV}v_i, v_j)$ and reports the mean reciprocal rank, contrasted against the same statistic on random directions so that a head copying everything indiscriminately scores zero.

[[broadcast-heads]] are then the top 1% of workspace-layer heads scored by the worse of their two ranks. A head must do both things to qualify.

Six populations were run through the same selection. One of them is the lens vectors under a fixed random orthogonal rotation, which preserves their spectrum and their pairwise geometry while destroying their identity; it is the control that separates being J-space directions from merely being that shape. The heads selected for the lens vectors separate cleanly from every comparison population on both metrics ([[fig-33]]), and they concentrate in the first half of the band, where the J-space's effective rank is lowest and one OV map can carry more of it.

The ablation zeroes those heads at every position, against equal-sized layer-matched random heads over five seeds. Recall@25 is the fraction of the unablated run's top-25 lens tokens still in the top 25 afterwards, and at the worst mid-workspace layers it falls to 0.67 against the control's 0.86, while the top-1 next token changes at 5% of positions against 2% ([[fig-34]]).

The behavioral checks are where the dissociation bites. Reporting of an injected thought falls from 0.54 to 0.09 while the control leaves it intact ([[fig-7]]), and on the [[experiential-reports]] prompts the head ablation reproduces roughly a third of the drop caused by full [[j-space-ablation]].

chapters.title: Committing to one reading
chapters.body:
The [[embedding-mixture-experiment]] manufactures ambiguity at the input rather than looking for it. A concept token's input embedding is replaced by the mixture $(1-\alpha)\,e_B + \alpha\,e_A$ inside an ordinary carrier sentence, sixteen pairs of single-token country names across forty sentences, with $\alpha$ swept from 0 to 1 and the residual stream recorded at that position at every layer.

The first readout deliberately avoids the lens. [[projection-share]] places the activation on the line joining the same trial's pure-$B$ activation to its pure-$A$ activation, at the same position and layer, so the ends of the sweep sit at 0 and 1 by construction. Early layers track $\alpha$ smoothly; from about layer 38 the value sits near one end or the other and switches at a threshold ([[fig-29]]).

[[transition-width]] puts a number on the switch: the change in $\alpha$ needed to move the share from 10% to 90%. It falls steeply over roughly layers 21 to 42. Measured separately for the component along the two concepts' lens directions and for the complement with the top sixteen lens vectors projected out, the J-space component is consistently narrower and reaches its floor earlier ([[fig-70]]).

An average sitting mid-way admits two readings. Every trial might be genuinely undecided, or trials might each commit and split evenly.

[[bimodal-commitment]] separates them. At the most ambiguous $\alpha$, the per-trial shares pile up near 0 and near 1 ([[fig-71]]). At early layers both components sit near 0.5; by mid-depth the J-space component is clearly bimodal while its complement still has mass in the middle.

What this licenses is narrow. The sharpening is an analog of [[ignition]] in timing and shape, measured on artificial blended embeddings, and it corroborates the [[layer-bands]] boundary without using the lens to do so.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--the-t.title: Four Theories and One Exclusion
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--the-t.intro: The level above gave each theory its verdict. This one gives each verdict the evidence it rests on: which experiment was pointed at, what number came back, and where the paper marks its own case as thin.

chapters.title: The ground rules before any scoring
chapters.body:
The exercise is not framed as a test for consciousness. It is framed as a contribution to [[indicator-properties]], a proposal that an AI system be assessed by measuring properties drawn from several scientific [[theories-of-consciousness]] at once, rather than by picking a winning theory and applying it alone. The properties come from [[global-workspace-theory]], [[higher-order-theories|higher-order theories]], [[attention-schema-theory]], [[recurrent-processing-theory]] and others.

What the paper offers that framework is a structure, not a verdict. Indicators stated as claims about a system's internal organization need something concrete to be checked against, and the [[j-space]] is concrete: the [[jacobian-lens]] reads it, and interventions act on it.

The paper also expects traffic in the other direction. It suspects its results may bear on the theories themselves, by exhibiting a system that displays some of the properties associated with conscious access through mechanisms that differ from the ones those theories posit.

One family of accounts is placed outside the exercise entirely. [[substrate-dependent-theories]] hold that consciousness turns on properties of the brain beyond its functional or computational organization: its physical causal structure, or its biological substrate. The paper's experiments concern the computations a language model performs, not the hardware that performs them.

The consequence is a statement of scope rather than a result. Against those theories the findings are declared not relevant, which is different from negative. Nothing measured here counts for or against them.

The restriction also fixes what the four remaining chapters can be. Every theory checked below ties consciousness to function, so every one of them can be argued with using measurements. Whether functional signatures settle anything about [[phenomenal-consciousness]] is set aside from the paper's first page; what it studies is [[access-consciousness]].

chapters.title: Global workspace theory, with numbers attached
chapters.body:
[[global-workspace-theory]] supplied the design brief, so what is left to say is how each of its claims became a measurement.

Capacity was measured twice. [[j-space-occupancy]] fits the residual stream with a sparse non-negative combination of $K$ lens vectors, and reports the $K$ at which adding one more vector stops beating a same-size set of random directions. That count is near zero through the first third of the layers and plateaus around 25 across the [[workspace-layers]]. Holding $K$ at that median, the variance those directions explain in excess of the random control never exceeds 10%. The [[word-list-experiment]] gives the functional version of the same limit: on an eighty-word list of unrelated words, only about six of the words read so far are present at any comma, and at a single layer the figure is closer to one or two. So [[j-space-capacity]] is small in two senses, in share of the representation and in number of items.

Breadth was measured on the weights. [[mlp-gain]] asks how strongly the next [[mlp-block]] amplifies a direction, normalized against random directions. Lens vectors reach roughly ten times through the workspace band, while the output directions of individual MLP neurons stay near one ([[fig-32]]). Across positions, [[broadcast-heads]] are the top one percent of workspace-layer heads by relay quality. [[broadcast-head-ablation]] drops readout recall to 0.67 against 0.86 for random heads, and changes the top-1 next token at only 5% of positions. That pairing is what makes [[j-space-broadcast]] a claim about the workspace rather than about the output.

Sharpness was measured on ambiguous inputs. The [[embedding-mixture-experiment]] blends two country embeddings and sweeps the blend; early layers track it smoothly, and from layer 38 the activation sits at one end or the other ([[ignition]]).

The weak point is implementation. Brain broadcast runs on recurrent loops and long-range cortical connections. A forward pass has neither, and the paper does not claim to know whether that matters.
chapters.childScope: Take each global-workspace analog down to its own measurement and controls: [[j-space-capacity]] through [[j-space-occupancy]] and the [[word-list-experiment]] with [[category-displacement]]; [[j-space-broadcast]] through [[mlp-gain]], [[broadcast-heads]], [[label-preservation]] and [[broadcast-head-ablation]]; and [[ignition]] through the [[embedding-mixture-experiment]] and [[bimodal-commitment]].

chapters.title: Higher-order theories and the shape of blindsight
chapters.body:
Self-descriptive readouts do appear in the lens: thinking, focused. The paper does not build on them, because it says they are not the norm. The case it presses for [[higher-order-theories]] is structural, and it rests on the selectivity experiments.

[[blindsight]] is the reference case. Visual information presented to a damaged field still shapes behavior, and a patient can guess the location of a stimulus above chance while reporting no awareness of having seen anything. The higher-order reading is that the information is represented in a first-order sense and not in a higher-order one.

The paper's two selectivity experiments do not have the same shape, and the difference matters for the analogy. In the [[language-passage-tasks]] battery, the passage's language appears in the readouts at comparable rates under all four tasks. A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] exchanging Spanish for French flips the named answer and the flexible inferences, while the continuation stays in Spanish and the spliced foreign sentence is still detected. There the information is in the workspace and causally inert for the routine tasks.

The [[linewrap-task]] is the closer parallel. Asked to keep wrapping lines, the model tracks a running character count, yet number tokens are absent from the lens across the whole prompt, and a swap mapping counts in the forties to the sixties leaves the wrap point where it was. Asked instead how many characters the first line holds, the model answers "46", numbers appear in the lens at twenty positions, and the same swap moves the answer to "65" ([[fig-21]]). [[selectivity]] here is a fact about what enters the workspace, not only about what is used once inside, which is what makes it look like the [[unconscious-processing]] the theory has in mind.

What the paper will not settle is whether the entering representation is higher-order at all, or merely more accessible. Computational variants cast the higher-order state as a pointer that tags a first-order state's reliability. The J-space instead re-encodes the content in words.

chapters.title: Attention schema theory: reports of the operating
chapters.body:
[[attention-schema-theory]] makes a claim about what a report is a report of. A system builds a simplified model of its own attention, and within that model attention is depicted as an act of subjective experience; what is available for report is the model, not the attentional state itself. Applied to a language model, the prediction is that the structure the model reports from carries a description of the operating, not only the thing operated on.

Three results are offered. In the [[experiential-reports]] experiments, the lens contents during stream-of-consciousness narration are dominated by the act itself: thinking appears in the top ten at 58% of position-and-layer slots, thoughts at 23%, feeling at 17%, conscious at 7%. The same words appear substantially less often in the output distribution at those positions, which is the check that they are not simply echoing the text being written. [[j-space-ablation]] over layers 38 to 54 removes the experiential register while the narration stays fluent ([[fig-25]]).

In [[directed-modulation]], the lens carries the instructed content, orange or seven or forty, and beside it [[metacognitive-representations]] naming the act: thinking, imagine, calculate, focused. These sit at earlier layers than the content, as though the operation is represented before its result.

The [[thought-suppression]] experiments go further. Across forty concepts, failure words and damn reach the lens top five on 93% and 82% of trials under the suppression instruction in the post-trained model, against 17% and 30% in the base model, and never at all under a matched positive instruction.

The paper marks its own limits twice. Those suppression words were not shown to be downstream of the failure rather than of the instruction. And none of this is a model of attention as such, which leaves the fit at the edge of what the theory predicts. Widening from attention to self-modeling, the tokens AI, assistant, bot and chat surface at the start of the Assistant's turn independently of the prompt ([[assistant-point-of-view]]).

chapters.title: Recurrent processing theory: depth in place of loops
chapters.body:
[[recurrent-processing-theory]] is the one theory whose verdict looks settled before any measurement. A single [[feedforward-sweep]] is unconscious however far it propagates, and a representation becomes conscious only once later areas feed back to earlier ones. A [[transformer]] has no recurrence within a forward pass, so on its face the architecture is ruled out.

The paper's reply concerns where the theory came from. Its empirical motivation is timing: conscious perception takes longer than the feedforward sweep alone, and a stimulus must be processed for some minimum duration before it can be reported on. Recurrence is how a brain extends processing past one sweep given fixed anatomy.

Read that way, the operative computational property is serial processing depth, and recurrence is the brain's means of buying it rather than the thing itself.

Depth is what a transformer has instead, and it has it along one of its [[two-time-dimensions]]. The early region identified by the [[layer-bands]] analysis, before the workspace begins, is offered as the functional analog: a representation must pass through some number of stages before it enters the workspace. Whether those stages are stacked in a feedforward net or produced by looping over a shallower one may be an implementation detail rather than a difference in kind. Related work on [[feedforward-emulation-of-recurrence]] supports the exchange, since a feedforward stack can reproduce a recurrent network's computation up to as many steps as it has layers.

Two things sit against this. The reply is an argument, not an experiment, and no measurement in the paper tests it.

And the paper says elsewhere that it does not know why the early band is empty. The content may genuinely require depth to form. Or the lens, whose [[averaged-jacobian]] relates each layer to the final layer, may simply fail to read a region that far from the end.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.title: The Oracle Lens, Stage by Stage
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.intro: Four stages were named above. This level walks them in order: what each one is fitted against, why the dictionary used to train the oracle does not limit what the oracle can say, and where the single accuracy number comes from. The figure that closes the span is nine hand-picked prompts, and its display conventions decide how much they carry.

chapters.title: Learning to write a template vector
chapters.body:
The [[template-lens]] builds a direction for a word by hand. Claude writes a few hundred short passages that end just before the word, the model is run over them, and the residual stream at the final position is averaged, centered and whitened ([[template-construction]]). Every word costs its own batch of passages, which is exactly why the vocabulary has to be fixed in advance.

The [[reconstructor-model]] replaces that batch with a single forward pass. It is a copy of the subject model, fine-tuned so that a short phrase of text goes in and the [[residual-stream]] vector that would sit immediately before that phrase comes out. A per-word construction becomes a function that accepts any string.

Training pairs cost nothing to collect, because ordinary text already contains them. A position is sampled from Assistant-turn text. The next $N$ tokens are taken as the phrase, with $N$ drawn uniformly from one to thirty-two. The [[activations]] of the residual stream at the preceding position are taken as the target.

The loss is [[cosine-similarity|cosine]] error in the whitened metric the template lens already uses. Equivalently, it is mean-squared error between the unit-normalized $\Sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}}$-whitened prediction and the whitened target. Whitening divides out the directions the residual stream varies along anyway, so a prediction earns nothing for landing near the bulk of activation space. Normalizing discards scale, so the reconstructor is asked for a direction and only a direction.

Every later stage of the [[oracle-lens]] operates in that whitened space, and the experiments run on [[claude-model-family|Haiku 4.5]]. A figure reported later as variance explained is therefore whitened variance, not raw.

chapters.title: A dictionary that exists only to teach
chapters.body:
The finished oracle is meant to emit arbitrary phrases, so [[oracle-training]] needs supervision that is itself arbitrary-phrase shaped. The dictionary built in the second stage supplies that supervision. It never constrains what the oracle can output; it exists to label training data and is then done.

Construction is enumeration rather than learning. Roughly one million start positions are sampled from a held-out corpus of Assistant-turn text. At each, the 2-, 4-, 8-, 16- and 32-token continuation is taken, which is five million phrases before duplicates are removed. Deduplicating within each length leaves roughly 3.4 million, and every one is passed through the reconstructor to obtain its direction. Nothing here resembles the unsupervised optimization behind a [[sparse-autoencoder]] dictionary.

The third stage uses that dictionary to label activations. A teacher decomposes each of one million held-out Assistant-turn activations against it by non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit. The procedure is greedy: it repeatedly adds the entry that best explains what is so far unexplained, refits the coefficients of the chosen set, and holds every coefficient at or above zero. It belongs to the same family as the [[gradient-pursuit]] the paper runs over [[jacobian-lens|J-lens]] vectors elsewhere, with a different dictionary underneath it.

Two restrictions are imposed on the teacher. The decomposition runs one phrase length at a time, so a four-token phrase competes only against other four-token phrases. On each datapoint it is further restricted to a random half of the entries at that length, and the stated reason is that the distilled oracle cannot then memorize a fixed selection ranking over the dictionary.

For each activation the teacher records an ordered list of up to sixteen phrases, their fitted coefficients, and the fraction of whitened variance they explain. That list is the label ([[multi-token-lens-extensions]]).

chapters.title: Supervision, then reward, then a refit
chapters.body:
The fourth stage trains the oracle: a second fine-tuned copy of the subject model. The activation is injected into the oracle's residual stream, the prompt states the desired phrase length $N$ and count $K$, and the target is the teacher's first $K$ phrases at that length. This is distillation of a search into a generation. At inference the oracle emits a list directly, instead of running matching pursuit over 3.4 million entries.

Reinforcement learning then refines it on a fresh batch of Assistant-turn activations ([[rlhf]] is the familiar form of the same machinery, against a different reward). The reward is the fraction of whitened activation variance explained by the reconstructed directions of the generated list, with small format penalties for deviating from the target $K$ and $N$. Reward is therefore the evaluation metric itself rather than agreement with the teacher, and the oracle is free to propose phrases no dictionary entry ever matched. The published examples come from an RL-refined checkpoint.

Decoding an activation takes three steps. $K$ phrases are sampled from the oracle, each is mapped back to a direction by the reconstructor, and the coefficients are recovered by a non-negative least-squares refit against the original activation. The oracle's own sense of how much each phrase matters is not used; the weights beside a readout come from a fit against the real vector.

The accuracy is 31% of whitened variance on average, over Assistant-turn positions of a held-out corpus of on-policy transcripts. No baseline is set beside it in this section. It is also not the paper's other variance number: [[excess-variance-explained]] measures something different, the margin of the top J-lens vectors over a random control.

The cost is two auxiliary fine-tuned models, which the paper states plainly makes the [[oracle-lens]] substantially more expensive than either other lens ([[readout-method-tradeoffs]], [[j-lens-readout]], [[free-text-activation-decoders]]).
