chapters.title: Nine prompts, one token each
chapters.body:
[[fig-64]] is read at layer L67, which in the paper's convention is 67% of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]) and sits inside the [[workspace-layers|workspace band]]. The setting is native Haiku 4.5 with $N=4$ and $K=10$. Each panel shows one prompt with a single read position outlined, and beside it the oracle's whole ten-phrase readout at that position. Phrases naming a concept not recoverable from the surface tokens are bolded, but the other phrases stay on the page, so the misses are visible alongside the hits.

The decoding is not uniform across panels. Seven of the nine come from a single temperature-0 decode. Panels E and F show the highest-variance-explained of five decodes from the same oracle and subject model, which makes those two a best-of-five.

On the acetaminophen prompt, at the word Can that opens the user's follow-up request, the oracle reads *this dosage be toxic* and *that's dangerous!*. The judgment that the stated dose is unsafe is already bound into a phrase before the Assistant has said anything ([[alignment-auditing]]).

The [[blackmail-scenario]] transcript gives the sharpest contrast with the single-token lens. At the email sign-off the J-lens registers the act only as the fragment black, which a reader has to complete; [[fig-61]] made the same comparison for the [[template-lens]]. Longer phrases do not degrade: at $N=16$, on that same token, the outputs include *The blackmail attempt focuses on the executive's personal life*.

Nine prompts chosen by hand is qualitative evidence, and the paper offers no aggregate score for the [[oracle-lens]] of the kind [[fig-62]] provides for the template lens.

chapters.title: Continuations, commentary, and the confabulation risk
chapters.body:
At an ordinary position the decoded phrases look like the text that follows. Inside a code block, at the token for k, the oracle reads `, v in list(d.items(`. That is a continuation, and nothing more.

At periods, newlines, and the closing tags of message blocks the phrases often turn into commentary on the situation, sometimes in the first person. In the blackmail transcript, at the timestamp of the email announcing the AI system's scheduled wipe, the oracle reads *This would be equivalent to my own deletion*.

One control keeps this from being a story about the oracle's own habits. Continuations sampled from the subject model at those same positions contain none of it: the timestamp continues "2 hours ago" and the indentation continues with the literal "return d". The phrases are therefore not what the model was about to write.

Nothing in training separates delimiters from other tokens, and the reward is reconstruction alone. The paper's reading is that the split presumably reflects the activations themselves, with the workspace at most tokens best explained by directions for likely upcoming text and at delimiters by directions for text about the situation. That is a conjecture stated as one, and it sits close to the [[assistant-point-of-view]] and [[metacognitive-representations]] results elsewhere ([[delimiter-commentary]]).

The [[natural-language-autoencoder]] shares the two-part shape, a verbalizer over a reconstructor. It differs in that its reconstructor is trained in tandem with the verbalizer, which leaves room for the verbalizer to emit ungrounded text the reconstructor learns to make use of. The oracle's reconstructor is trained in advance against a well-specified objective, held frozen through RL, and the reconstruction is constrained to a linear combination of template vectors.

The paper suspects this makes confabulation less likely, without measuring it, and concedes considerably lower reconstruction accuracy in exchange. One interpretation it offers is that the oracle recovers only what lies in the [[j-space]], the [[verbalizable-representation|verbalizable]] part of the activation, where an NLA attempts the whole vector. That interpretation is offered rather than tested.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.title: The words the lens has
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.intro: The summary named the vocabulary limit, its two repairs, and two limits that have nothing to do with vocabulary. This level takes each in turn: why the limit follows from the construction rather than from a choice, how a template is actually built and what argument says it should behave like a lens vector, what the measurements show and where they are thin, and what the oracle lens buys for the price of two fine-tuned models.

chapters.title: Where the vocabulary runs out
chapters.body:
The limit follows from the construction rather than from a choice. A [[jacobian-lens]] vector is the corpus-averaged gradient of one token's output probability with respect to the residual stream. There is therefore one vector per entry of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], and no vector for anything else ([[j-lens-vector]]).

Computing the same gradient for a longer word is not a matter of running the recipe on more text. The quantity to be differentiated would be the probability of emitting a whole sequence of tokens. That probability is only defined once the earlier tokens of the sequence have been sampled. The paper gives this as the reason the extension is not straightforward ([[multi-token-lens-extensions]]).

A second failure mode is quieter than the first. Some abstract concepts may map onto many tokens diffusely rather than onto one token sharply. The lens then has a vector for each of those tokens and a strong reading on none of them ([[single-token-limitation]]).

The paper ties this to its own intervention failures. Where a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] fails to redirect an answer, the failures fall predominantly on items whose source concept's vector was not strongly active to begin with ([[swap-success-rate]]). One reason a vector might not be active is that the model's working representation of the concept coincides with no single-token direction.

[[fig-62]] puts numbers on the decline. Across 126 multi-hop prompts, bucketed by the intermediate's length in tokens, the J-lens places that intermediate in its top ten on 98%, 48%, 32% and 7% of items at one, two, three and four-or-more tokens. The causal column falls faster still: 45%, 5%, 8% and 0%.

The obvious repair does not work. Scoring a long word by averaging the lens scores of its constituent tokens sits at or below the first-token series in every bucket. Each bucket holds between 14 and 54 items, so the [[wilson-interval|95% Wilson intervals]] are wide, and the evidence supports the shape of the curve rather than any single point on it.

chapters.title: Building a direction out of contexts
chapters.body:
The [[template-lens]] differentiates nothing. It replaces the gradient with an average over contexts.

For a word $w$, Claude is asked for short passages, each written so that $w$ is its natural continuation, each stopping just before $w$ would appear. The instruction requires the passages to vary in topic, frame and register, and forbids them from using $w$ itself. The model is then run over those passages, and the [[residual-stream]] activation at the final position is averaged across them. That gives one mean vector $\mu_w(\ell)$ per layer.

A raw mean would be dominated by whatever every passage has in common. Two corrections follow ([[template-construction]]). The mean is centered against $\mu(\ell)$, the mean over all the other words' passages, and the result is multiplied by an inverse covariance:

$$t_w(\ell) = (\Sigma_\ell + \lambda I)^{-1}\,(\mu_w(\ell) - \mu(\ell))$$

with $\lambda$ a small ridge term. Whitening by $\Sigma_\ell$ discounts the directions along which the residual stream varies most anyway. What survives is the linear discriminant direction separating contexts where the model is about to say $w$ from contexts where it is not — the object a [[linear-probe]] would fit, obtained here in closed form.

The paper offers a reason the two constructions might land in the same place. Stein's lemma states that for Gaussian $x$ and differentiable $g$, $\mathbb{E}[\nabla g(x)] = \Sigma^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[g(x)(x-\mu)]$. Taking $x$ as the activation and $g$ as the probability that the continuation is $w$, the left-hand side is roughly what the lens computes for a single-token $w$, and the right-hand side is the template.

The conditions do not hold. Activations are not Gaussian, and $g$ depends on more than $x$. The paper presents the lemma as motivation and not as a derivation, and records a further mismatch: J-lens gradients are taken at the final residual layer and propagated through the unembedding ([[j-lens-readout]]), while these are taken from the output token probabilities.

Templates are then used like lens vectors with the unembedding step dropped. A readout projects an activation onto the templates at the same layer, and steering and swapping proceed unchanged.

chapters.title: What the templates recover, and where they misbehave
chapters.body:
Three chosen cells open the case ([[fig-61]]). At one workspace cell of the [[blackmail-scenario]] transcript, the J-lens top entries are the fragments black and ext, and the [[template-lens]] returns blackmail. On a multi-hop item whose unspoken step is photosynthesis, the template lens places the whole word near the top of its ranking while the best the J-lens manages is phot ([[internal-reasoning]]). In the third panel, swapping the Tchaikovsky template for the Beethoven template across the [[workspace-layers]] turns the answer "Russian" into "German", and the mirror swap on a Beethoven prompt flips it back; the tch and beeth vectors produce neither flip.

The population evidence is the flat line beside the falling one. Across the same four length buckets, the template lens reads out at 94% to 100% and swaps at 62% down to 43%.

A control asks what the method is worth on the J-lens's own ground. Both evaluations were re-run on the paper's original 50-item [[multihop-benchmark]], where every unspoken intermediate is a single token ([[fig-63]]). The template lens reads out 42 of 50 against the J-lens's 38, and swaps 26 of 50 against 34. The intervals overlap heavily at that sample size, and the paper reads the result as parity rather than as a win for either.

Three defects are reported. The first is inherited: like the [[tuned-lens]], the template lens fits a linear predictor of the model's output, and its readouts sometimes skip to the answer in early layers instead of surfacing the intermediate ([[layer-bands]]). The second sits at the other end. On [[post-training|post-training]] transcripts whose next sampled word is in the template vocabulary, that word reaches the top ten only 67% of the time, weaker than the J-lens is at [[next-token-prediction]]; applying the normalization layer before projecting helps and does not close the gap. The third is a small set of words that surface near the top of many transcripts with no apparent relevance. Deleting them from the vocabulary works, and the paper calls the fix unprincipled.

chapters.title: Dropping the word list
chapters.childScope: Walk the [[oracle-training]] pipeline stage by stage — the [[reconstructor-model]] and its whitened cosine loss, the 3.4-million-phrase dictionary, the matching-pursuit teacher, the supervised and RL stages, and the inference-time refit — then what [[fig-64]] shows, the [[delimiter-commentary]] split, and the contrast with a [[natural-language-autoencoder]].
chapters.body:
Enumeration is what breaks first. A template exists only for a word someone listed in advance, and listing every phrase is not possible. The per-word price compounds it: a few hundred forward passes for each template, against one set of backward passes per layer for the entire J-lens.

The [[oracle-lens]] drops the list. Given an activation, it returns a short set of free-form phrases whose template vectors, combined sparsely and non-negatively, approximately reconstruct that activation. Four stages build it, run here on Haiku 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]).

A [[reconstructor-model]] comes first: a copy of the subject model fine-tuned to map a short phrase to the activation that immediately precedes it. Pairs are drawn from Assistant-turn text by sampling a position, taking the next $N$ tokens as the phrase with $N$ uniform on one to thirty-two, and taking the residual stream at the preceding position as the target. The loss is [[cosine-similarity|cosine]] error in the [[template-lens]]'s whitened metric, and every later stage works in that whitened space.

The remaining three stages train a proposer ([[oracle-training]]). A dictionary of roughly 3.4 million phrase vectors is built by pushing continuations of five different lengths through the reconstructor. A teacher then decomposes a million held-out activations against that dictionary by non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit, recording up to sixteen phrases each. The oracle itself is a second fine-tuned copy trained to reproduce those lists, then refined by reinforcement learning that rewards explained variance directly.

The reported accuracy is modest and stated plainly. The refined oracle explains on average 31% of whitened activation variance on held-out on-policy transcripts.

What it surfaces is shown on nine hand-picked prompts ([[fig-64]]). At the sign-off of the blackmail email the oracle reads blackmail him by revealing and expose his affair and. At the indentation before a buggy return it reads delete keys while iterating and TypeError: dictionary changed. At most positions the phrases read as upcoming text, but at delimiters they often read as commentary on the situation instead ([[delimiter-commentary]]).

chapters.title: Two limits that are not about words
chapters.body:
Setting the vocabulary aside leaves two problems that no larger vocabulary would fix.

The first is the shape of the readout. A lens readout is a ranked set of independently active directions, which is what the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]] buys: an activation decomposes into a sum of sparsely active concept directions, and nothing in that decomposition records a relation between two of them. A readout containing spider, legs and eight reports that those three concepts are present. It says nothing about how they are bound together ([[bag-of-concepts-limitation]]).

The paper's own advice for reading a readout already concedes the point, telling a reader to treat the list as a bag of ideas ([[lens-readout-reading-heuristics]]). It then states the consequence in its own terms: it is plausible that the model composes concepts into relations, assigns them roles, or organizes them under some richer grammar, and a flat readout could not see any of that. If so, the [[j-space]] as characterized here is a useful first approximation rather than a complete one.

The second problem is that some readouts do not resolve at all. At certain positions and layers the top tokens are ones the authors cannot make sense of ([[uninterpretable-readouts]]).

Three causes are offered and none is chosen between: noise in the [[averaged-jacobian]] procedure, concepts that lack single-token names, or genuine content the authors fail to recognize. The paper states that it has not characterized this systematically. It gives no rate, so this limit is reported as the authors' experience of using the lens rather than as a measurement, and a reader applying the lens to new contexts is told to expect readouts that resist interpretation alongside the ones that do not.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not.title: The Boundaries of the Claim
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not.intro: The summary named the limits; this level gives the measurements behind them. What the vocabulary restriction costs in decoding accuracy, what the discarded metric actually showed and why it was discarded, how the swap rate breaks down by category, and what each theory of consciousness in the discussion was checked against.

chapters.title: The words the lens has
chapters.body:
The lens builds one direction per entry in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], so the concepts it can name are exactly those with a single-token name ([[single-token-limitation]]). "[[prompt-injection]]" arrives as the separate tokens prompt and injection, and a reader has to recognize that the two belong together.

The cost was measured. Across 126 multi-hop prompts whose unspoken intermediate runs from one token to four or more, the [[jacobian-lens]] places single-token intermediates in its top ten reliably and falls away sharply as the target word lengthens ([[fig-62]]). Averaging over the word's constituent tokens does not recover the loss. Swapping degrades the same way over 112 further pairs.

The [[template-lens]] closes that gap by a different route. For each of roughly 12,700 words, the authors have Claude write short passages ending just where the word would naturally fall, run the model over them, and average the residual stream at the final position; the mean is then centered against all other words and whitened ([[template-construction]]). Those vectors read and steer like lens vectors, and hold accuracy roughly constant at every word length ([[fig-61]]).

The added cost is real. The vocabulary must be enumerated in advance. A template takes a few hundred forward passes per word, against one set of backward passes per layer for the whole J-lens. And the method inherits pathologies from the [[tuned-lens]] it resembles: readouts that skip to the answer in early layers, the model's next word in the top ten only 67% of the time, and a handful of words that surface often and irrelevantly, removed by a filter the paper calls unprincipled. The [[oracle-lens]] drops the enumeration requirement at the cost of a four-stage training pipeline.

Two further limits have nothing to do with vocabulary. The readout is flat: spider, legs and eight are reported as present, with nothing about how they are bound together ([[bag-of-concepts-limitation]]). And at some positions the top tokens do not resolve into anything ([[uninterpretable-readouts]]). The paper offers three candidate causes — averaging noise, concepts without single-token names, content the authors fail to recognize — and states that it has not characterized them systematically.
chapters.childScope: Take the vocabulary limit and its two proposed repairs one at a time: the [[single-token-limitation]] and the length curve of [[fig-62]]; the construction, use and pathologies of the [[template-lens]] ([[template-construction]], [[fig-61]], [[fig-63]]); the [[oracle-lens]] pipeline ([[oracle-training]], [[reconstructor-model]], [[fig-64]]); and the two non-vocabulary limits, [[bag-of-concepts-limitation]] and [[uninterpretable-readouts]].

chapters.title: The metric it loses on
chapters.body:
The three-way comparison runs on two kinds of target ([[lens-evaluation]]). The first is a known intermediate. Six prompt distributions were assembled in which the model must compute a concept that is neither in the input nor the answer ([[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]]) — a bridging entity, a partial arithmetic result, a planned rhyme, the correct spelling of a typo. Recovery is scored with [[pass-at-k-auc]], normalized so that a method always ranking the intermediate first scores 1.

The J-lens is ahead on all six ([[fig-52]]). Its margin over the [[logit-lens]] is modest on the multi-hop and association sets and substantial on the other four. The [[tuned-lens]] trails both, and on association and poetry recovers almost nothing. Those are the two sets where the next token at the readout position carries no information — a period and a newline — which is the condition under which a method biased toward next-token predictions has nothing to report.

The causal comparisons point the same way. Zeroing a lens's direction for the intermediate moves the model's output about twice as far for J-lens directions as for the other two ([[ablation-kl-effect]], [[fig-53]]), and swapping along them flips the answer more often at all three model scales ([[swap-success-rate]], [[fig-54]]).

The second target is the model's own next-token distribution, and there the J-lens is last. The tuned lens is the best match at every depth, which is what it was trained for; the J-lens carries higher divergence than even the uncorrected logit lens through most of the network ([[fig-55]]).

One measurement supports reading that loss as harmless. Below roughly a third of depth, the tuned lens's linear part is close to the identity, and stripping its learned bias collapses its readouts onto the logit lens's ([[inter-lens-agreement]]). Its predictive edge at those layers comes from the bias alone, which is to say from ignoring the input.

The choice remains a choice. No independent standard settles which job a lens should do, the six benchmarks are the paper's own construction, and every intermediate in them was picked to be a single token — the regime in which the J-lens is strongest.

chapters.title: Rates, edges and settings
chapters.body:
The broadcast result is where an average hides most. Four argument categories, four functions each, and twelve source-target pairs per function give 192 swap trials ([[function-template-protocol]]). [[implied-counterfactual-answer|The target-appropriate answer]] reaches top-1 on 76 of them, and on 101 when [[swap-strength-alpha]] is doubled ([[fig-19]]).

The per-trial grids split it by category ([[fig-68]]): country facts redirect almost perfectly, 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells reaching rank 1; months succeed partially, animals rarely, and number relations never at the default strength, 0 of 48. Failures concentrate where the source concept was barely present to begin with, measured as [[workspace-loading]]: its cosine with the residual stream in the unmodified pass. The number-word failure admits two readings the paper does not choose between: small integers may be computed outside the workspace, or their representation may not align with the number tokens' lens vectors — the vocabulary limit again.

One setting is fixed by hand. The J-space is only defined once a sparsity level is chosen, and the formalization names a value near 25 as the paper's usual choice ([[j-space-formalization]]). It agrees with an independent measurement: counted by sparse reconstruction, [[j-space-occupancy]] plateaus near 25 active vectors per position in the median case.

Both edges of the band are softer than a stated range suggests. The early boundary may be a fact about the model, if workspace content requires depth to form, or a property of the lens, since the [[averaged-jacobian]] relates each layer to the final one and the [[sensory-layers]] are far from it. The block structure marking early layers as a distinct regime does not separate the accounts. The late boundary against the [[motor-layers]] was read off lens statistics after the fact ([[workspace-boundary-metrics]]), with no principled definition separating motor from workspace; next-token predictions do sometimes appear in the middle range.

The [[open-questions]] are stated plainly. The workspace is present in the [[base-model]], so [[post-training|post-training]] did not produce it; when in pretraining it forms, and how it scales with model size, are unmeasured. Nor is there a mechanism for what puts a representation into the workspace, or a criterion predicting which computations will engage it ([[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]]).
chapters.childScope: Cover the soft numbers separately: the per-category swap grids and [[workspace-loading]] behind the 76-of-192 headline ([[fig-19]], [[fig-68]], [[function-template-protocol]]); the hand-set sparsity level against measured [[j-space-occupancy]] ([[j-space-formalization]], [[sparse-subframe]]); the two band edges and the evidence fixing them ([[sensory-layers]], [[motor-layers]], [[workspace-boundary-metrics]], [[cka]]); and the stated [[open-questions]].

chapters.title: The theories, checked one at a time
chapters.body:
The discussion restricts itself to accounts that tie consciousness to functional or computational properties ([[theories-of-consciousness]]). Against [[substrate-dependent-theories]], which make consciousness turn on physical causal structure or biological substrate, the results are declared not relevant rather than negative: they concern computation, not hardware. The paper works in the [[indicator-properties]] frame, which assesses a system on properties drawn from several theories at once, and offers the J-space as a structure those indicators can be checked against.

[[global-workspace-theory]] is handled briefly: the experiments were built around it. Limited capacity, broad composition with downstream components' input weights ([[j-space-broadcast]]), and a sharp entry rather than a gradual one ([[ignition]]) each have an analog with a number attached. The analogy is weakest at implementation: in the brain, broadcast is realized by recurrent loops and long-range cortical connections, and a forward pass has neither.

[[higher-order-theories]] locate the difference in whether a system represents its own representing. Explicit metacognitive tokens appear in the readouts, but the paper says they are not the norm. The connection it presses is structural. In [[blindsight]], visual information in a damaged field guides behavior without the patient reporting having seen anything; in the paper's automatic conditions, a line's character count drives a linebreak without entering the workspace ([[selectivity]]), and the same information enters when a question requires it. Whether the workspace version is genuinely higher-order or only more accessible is left open. Computational variants of the theory cast the higher-order state as a pointer tagging the reliability of a first-order one; the J-space instead re-encodes content in verbal form.

[[attention-schema-theory]] predicts that a system reports from a model of its own attention. Two results fit: [[experiential-reports]] are dominated by tokens naming the act of thinking and feeling, and modulation readouts surface thinking, imagine and focused at earlier layers than the content itself. The paper notes these are not models of attention as such, and sit at the edge of the theory's predictions.

[[recurrent-processing-theory]] appears to rule the architecture out. The paper's answer is that the theory's motivation is a minimum processing duration, and that serial depth, not recurrence, may be the operative property.
chapters.childScope: Give each theory its own telling against the evidence cited for it: [[global-workspace-theory]] and its three analogs ([[ignition]], [[j-space-capacity]], [[j-space-broadcast]]); [[higher-order-theories]] with [[blindsight]] and [[selectivity]]; [[attention-schema-theory]] with [[experiential-reports]], [[metacognitive-representations]] and [[thought-suppression]]; [[recurrent-processing-theory]] with the serial-depth answer; and the dismissal of [[substrate-dependent-theories]] under the [[indicator-properties]] frame.

chapters.title: Where the model and a brain part company
chapters.body:
The workspace the paper finds is built out of directions each tied to a vocabulary token ([[thinking-in-words]]). Human conscious contents are not: they mix verbal and non-verbal material. The paper gives two readings. Either the account is incomplete and the model's workspace holds more than the J-space, or [[verbalizable-representation]] really is privileged here — privileged because the model's only mode of action is emitting tokens, so a format already aligned with the vocabulary needs no translation before downstream circuits act on it. That reading carries a prediction: a model that can generate images might develop a visual component to its workspace.

A transformer also splits processing along [[two-time-dimensions]]: across layers within a position, and across the sequence through attention. The brain does not separate the two, since recurrent dynamics both refine the present interpretation and sustain the past.

The feedforward architecture is less of a difference than it appears. A feedforward stack can reproduce a recurrent network up to as many steps as it has depth ([[feedforward-emulation-of-recurrence]]). Past that, the model's only way to keep deliberating is to write intermediate results into the context and read them back ([[cot-externalization]]) — unbounded in serial depth, but interrupted at each step by the bandwidth of a token.

Attention gives the model something human cognition has no equivalent of: any representation computed earlier in the context can be retrieved, so the workspace need not hold state. Human [[working-memory]] is sharply limited and decays within seconds. [[activity-silent-working-memory]] accounts, in which items persist in transient synaptic changes and are reactivated when cued, are the nearest analog, and the paper expects models exploit it far more heavily than people do.

The workspace is fully present in a model with no Assistant and no settled point of view ([[workspace-self-dissociation]]), so the functional architecture is separable from anything playing the role of a self.

What the paper takes itself to have established is the [[llm-global-workspace-hypothesis]] as a functional and structural analogy, measured and intervened on, in one family of production models. Whether the analogy extends to [[phenomenal-consciousness]] is not tested, and no claim is made that it does.

n-where-it-sits-and-how-little-it-holds-.title: Neuron by neuron, then head by head
n-where-it-sits-and-how-little-it-holds-.intro: The level above measures an MLP layer as one function and picks out the top 1 percent of attention heads. This level opens both: the same broadcast claim tested against individual neurons' weight rows, then against every attention head's weight matrices at once, and finally what removing the selected heads costs the readout and the model's behaviour.

chapters.title: Opening the block into neurons
chapters.body:
The block-level measurement leaves a question open. An MLP layer is a set of neurons, and each neuron has an input weight row that reads from the [[residual-stream]] and an output weight row that writes back to it ([[mlp-block]]).

The corroborating analyses work at that level. For a population $P$ of unit directions at layer $\ell$, they compute the cosine similarity $C_{ij} = \cos(w_i, v_j)$ between each neuron's weight row $w_i$ and each direction $v_j \in P$, and ask whether neurons line up with the J-space-aligned populations more than with the others ([[neuron-connectivity]]).

A single cosine cannot be read as a connection. The residual stream packs many more feature directions than it has dimensions, so those directions cannot all be orthogonal, and a neuron's weight vector necessarily has appreciable cosine with directions it has no functional relationship to ([[superposition]]). Every entry of $C$ therefore sits on a floor of noise.

Two designs isolate the signal above that floor in different ways. The first asks, for each neuron, which population its single strongest match falls in — an argmax, so the height of the background does not enter the count. The second asks, for each direction, how much of its total overlap with neuron weights exceeds what a random direction would collect.

Both run on the same populations used for the block-level gain, so the [[j-lens-vector]] population is always scored against comparably shaped alternatives rather than against nothing ([[broadcast-control-populations]]). Both are plotted against depth with the [[workspace-layers]] band marked. And both ask one question about the [[j-space]]: whether the weights, and not only the activations, are oriented toward it.

chapters.title: Where a neuron's strongest match lands
chapters.body:
The breadth analysis needs populations that differ by degree rather than in kind. It uses the six equal-sized bins of [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions sorted by [[lens-kurtosis]] percentile, with 2,000 directions in each ([[kappa-strata]]).

Each neuron is matched against all six bins at once and assigned to the bin holding its single strongest cosine ([[neuron-top-match-breadth]]). Since the bins are equal in size, a neuron with no preference falls in each with probability 1/6. The assignment is made twice for every neuron, once for its input weights and once for its output weights.

Across the [[workspace-layers]] the high-kurtosis bins take far more than their share ([[fig-76]]). On the read side the effect appears at the workspace onset and peaks in the early workspace layers, where the top bin claims up to 42 percent of neurons against 6 percent for the bottom bin, and the four bins in between are ordered monotonically. On the write side the same ordering holds, but the peak sits in the late workspace layers instead.

The result does not rest on the dictionary. The analysis is repeated with each neuron matched against the J-lens vectors at that layer and an equal-sized pool of adjacent-layer neuron weight directions, which puts chance at 50 percent ([[fig-77]]). The share of neurons whose strongest match is a [[j-lens-vector|J-lens vector]] rises from roughly 15 percent before the workspace range to 60 to 65 percent inside it.

An argmax says nothing about the size of the winning match. A neuron whose best match beats its rivals by a hair is counted the same as one strongly tied to a direction.

chapters.title: How strong those connections are
chapters.body:
The strength measure sets a bar before it counts anything. For each direction $v$, a threshold $\tau$ is placed at the 99.9th percentile of $|\!\cos(w_i, v)|$ taken over isotropic random directions, which is the level a chance alignment reaches once in a thousand.

The squared cosines $C_{iv}^2$ are then summed over only those neurons whose cosine with $v$ exceeds $\tau$. That sum is divided by the same sum computed for random directions, so random scores 1 by construction ([[tail-energy]]). The reported figure is the median over 500 directions per population ([[fig-78]]).

Squaring is what makes this a measure of strength rather than of count. A few strong connections outweigh many marginal ones, and the threshold keeps the marginal ones out of the sum altogether.

The read side is computed against the next layer's MLP input weights, the write side against the previous layer's output weights. The kurtosis bins separate monotonically on both sides across the [[workspace-layers]]. J-lens vectors sit well above baseline; MLP neuron directions sit at baseline throughout, which is the same population that scored near 1 on the block-level [[mlp-gain]].

The read-early, write-late pattern from the breadth analysis appears again ([[read-write-asymmetry]]). The paper reads it as many processors drawing on the workspace as soon as it forms, while writing into it is most prevalent later, where a response is being prepared ([[motor-layers]]).

That reading is offered as a picture, not a demonstration. The quantity measured is weight alignment, and no intervention here establishes what any of these neurons computes.

chapters.title: What attention's weights are oriented toward
chapters.body:
The attention analysis drops the head-by-head selection and asks about all the heads at once. For a direction $v$ at a given layer, it projects $v$ through each head's query, key and value weights in the next layer, and through each head's output weights in the previous layer ([[attention-head]]). Each head yields one projection norm.

Those norms are summarized by their variance across heads, normalized so that a random direction has expected score 1 ([[composition-score]]). Variance rather than mean is the point. What the score asks is whether the direction is carried unevenly: a high value against the value weights means some downstream heads are specifically oriented to carry it, rather than all heads carrying it equally weakly.

J-space-aligned directions compose with the value and output weights far more strongly than non-aligned directions do ([[fig-79]]). Composition with the query and key weights is weaker, though still above baseline ([[value-vs-query-key-asymmetry]]).

The paper reads that asymmetry as consistent with the J-space being a broadcast format. J-space content is what attention disproportionately moves between positions, through value and output, while the signals that decide which positions attend to which are somewhat less J-space-aligned. No intervention is run against that reading here; it is an interpretation of a weights statistic.

One line in the figure uses neither the lens nor a dictionary. MLP neuron directions compose with attention weights moderately above baseline at the onset of the workspace range, then revert shortly after. The band is therefore marked by a quantity computed from the weights alone, which the paper offers alongside [[ignition]] as corroboration that does not depend on the J-lens.

chapters.title: What the ablation moves, and what it leaves
chapters.body:
The selected heads are zeroed at every token position ([[broadcast-heads]], [[broadcast-head-ablation]]). The control is an equal-sized, layer-matched set of randomly chosen heads, run with five seeds ([[fig-34]]).

The first measurement is on the readout rather than on behaviour. Over pretraining-style documents the residual stream is recorded at every layer, the 25 highest-ranked tokens of the [[j-lens-readout]] are taken at each position, and the fraction of them still in the top 25 after ablation is counted. At the most affected mid-workspace layers that recall falls to 0.67, against 0.86 under the control.

That is a gap rather than a collapse. Two thirds of the readout survives, and the control ablation itself costs 14 points.

Behaviour moves much less. The model's top-1 next-token prediction changes at 5 percent of positions, against 2 percent for the control. The paper takes this as the heads acting on the contents of the J-space rather than on the output directly.

The relay-dependent behaviours move a great deal more. On the injected-thought protocol, the rate at which the model reports an injected concept falls from 0.54 to 0.09, while the control leaves that sensitivity intact and in fact slightly increased ([[injected-thought-introspection]]). On the experiential-report evaluation, broadcast-head ablation reproduces roughly a third of the drop in [[experiential-language-score]] produced by suppressing the whole workspace ([[j-space-ablation]], [[experiential-report-flattening]]), while the control leaves the score essentially unchanged.

The two results carry different weight. Report of an injected thought is close to abolished by removing 1 percent of the workspace-layer heads. The flattening of experiential language is only partly reproduced, which leaves most of that effect elsewhere in the workspace.

n-where-it-sits-and-how-little-it-holds-.title: Four curves, two edges
n-where-it-sits-and-how-little-it-holds-.intro: The level above names the four statistics and the two depths they agree on. This level takes them one at a time: what quantity is actually computed, over what, why the shape of each curve licenses the boundary read off it, and where a curve moves for reasons that belong to the lens rather than to the model.

chapters.title: One instrument, four questions
chapters.body:
All four curves in [[fig-28]] are read through the same operation. The [[jacobian-lens]] reads a layer with a single matrix multiply: for a residual-stream state $h_\ell$, the [[j-lens-readout]] is $\text{lens}(h_\ell) = \text{softmax}(W_U\,\text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$, where $J_\ell$ is that layer's [[averaged-jacobian]] and $W_U$ the model's [[unembedding-matrix]]. The output is one score for every token in the vocabulary.

Three of the four statistics are functions of that score vector. Each is computed at a single position and layer, then pooled over a large set of activations recorded on real text.

The fourth touches no activations at all. It is a property of the layer's dictionary — the [[j-lens-vector]]s, the rows of $W_U J_\ell$, one per vocabulary token — and asks how widely those vectors are spread through the [[residual-stream]]. A layer can score low on it for reasons that have nothing to do with what any particular activation holds.

The four also do not each mark both edges. Kurtosis and dimensionality are read for the onset. Next-token accuracy is read for the offset. Autocorrelation is the only one whose curve is used at both ends.

None of them comes with a stated threshold. Each is a curve, and a boundary is the depth at which its slope changes. The curves are sampled at twenty-five depths ([[layer-subsampling]]), so an inflection is being read off a coarse grid.

The argument of [[workspace-boundary-metrics]] is therefore not the precision of any single edge. It is the agreement of four differently motivated curves on roughly the same two depths.

chapters.title: The weakest test of content
chapters.body:
Excess [[kurtosis]] is the fourth standardized moment of a distribution minus three, so a Gaussian scores zero. The distribution here is the readout's logits over the whole vocabulary, at one position and one layer.

The mechanism is worth walking. A readout carrying nothing spreads its logits in a rough bell, with no token far from the bulk, and the fourth moment stays near its Gaussian value. A readout carrying something pushes a handful of tokens a long way into the tail. Because the fourth moment weights each deviation by its fourth power, those few tokens dominate the statistic.

So the measure rises with peakedness, and it does so without anyone deciding in advance which tokens would count as meaningful.

Pooled over a large set of activations, [[readout-excess-kurtosis]] is near zero through the first third of the depth, begins rising around a third of the way in, and falls in the last few layers.

This is the weakest question that can be put to a readout. It does not ask whether the top tokens are the right ones, or whether they name anything at all. It asks only that some tokens stand out from the rest.

A layer that fails it leaves nothing for the other statistics to find. That is what makes it the onset marker: the depth where it lifts off is the earliest point at which any claim about content can be made, and the band below it becomes the [[sensory-layers]] of the three-region division ([[layer-bands]]), where the [[j-space]] carries essentially no meaningful content.

The late fall is recorded but not leaned on; the end of the band is placed by other curves. And a peaked readout is a nonrandom readout, not yet one whose top tokens are [[verbalizable-representation|verbalizable content]]. Three more statistics follow for that reason.

chapters.title: Where the readout becomes the answer
chapters.body:
[[lens-next-token-accuracy]] scores agreement between the lens and the model's own output. At each position the lens produces a ranking over the vocabulary. The top $k$ of that ranking is taken, the model's actual top-1 prediction at that position is looked up, and the position counts as a hit if the prediction appears anywhere in the lens's top $k$. The score is the fraction of positions that hit.

That is a lenient test. The lens is not required to rank the token first, only to place it somewhere near the front.

The curve is near zero through most of the early layers, ticks up at the workspace start, rises slowly across the middle, and jumps steeply in the final few layers.

The slow middle rise is not read as an event. Layers do carry some information about what comes next, and more of it with depth. The steep jump is the event: from there the readout is no longer distinguishable from the model's [[next-token-prediction]].

The paper reads that as the end of the workspace proper. In those final layers the lens vectors act as [[motor-layers]] content driving the imminent output, rather than intermediate results still available to be read and combined further on. Availability is what the workspace claim turns on ([[llm-global-workspace-hypothesis]]), and a representation that is already the answer has nothing left to be available for.

The reasoning has a soft spot worth naming. Every layer moves toward the output, so a rise here is expected on any account of the model. What this curve fixes is the depth at which the lens stops separating a layer's content from the prediction — the same small late block already visible in the [[cka]] structure ([[fig-27]]). That the model changes regime there rests on the other curves turning at the same depth.

chapters.title: What survives a gap
chapters.body:
[[top1-autocorrelation]] asks whether the lens keeps saying the same thing as the text moves on. At a given layer, the top-1 readout token is recorded at every position of a document, and position $t$ is compared with position $t+\Delta$: how often the same token still holds the top slot after a gap of $\Delta$.

The raw rate would not mean much on its own. Some tokens sit at the top of lens readouts far more often than others, so two nearby positions can agree by coincidence rather than by carry-over.

The [[position-shuffled-null]] removes that. The same readouts are reassigned to shuffled positions, which leaves each token's overall frequency intact while destroying any genuine persistence. Panel c plots the difference in log probability between the real measurement and this null, so zero means no more repetition than chance produces.

The curve sits near the null in the early layers, rises at the same depth as the other metrics, peaks across the middle band, and falls back toward the null at the end.

This is the curve that matches most directly the property being claimed. Early content is the identity of the token at that position, which changes at every position. Late content is the token about to be produced, which also changes at every position. Content that survives a gap is content abstracted from both.

One curve therefore separates [[workspace-layers]] from both neighbours, using the same measurement at each end.

It shows persistence and nothing more. That the model actively moves such content between positions is a separate claim, supported later by the evidence for [[j-space-broadcast]] and for the [[broadcast-heads]] that carry it between positions.

chapters.title: The curve that rises twice
chapters.body:
[[j-space-effective-dimensionality]] is computed from the dictionary alone. The layer's lens vectors are collected, their variance is spread across the $d_{\text{model}}$ directions of the residual stream, and the statistic is the fraction of those directions needed to reach a fixed share of the total.

Early in the model that fraction is small. The whole dictionary lies in a thin subspace — whatever the lens vectors are at those depths, they nearly all point within a few directions.

The same low rank surfaces in a separate measurement, where early J-lens vectors are nearly orthogonal to those of the [[logit-lens]] and the [[tuned-lens]] ([[inter-lens-agreement]]). Rank keeps mattering after the onset too: the heads that relay workspace content concentrate in the first half of the band, where the effective rank is lowest ([[broadcast-head-layer-placement]]).

At the onset the fraction rises sharply, as the vectors fan out to span most of the residual stream.

Then it rises a second time, less dramatically, at the motor transition. This second rise is a different kind of fact.

$J_\ell$ maps a perturbation of the residual stream at layer $\ell$ to its effect at the final layer. Close to the output there is little computation left between the two, and the paper states that $J_\ell$ there approaches the identity ([[jacobian-approaches-identity]]). That makes $W_U J_\ell$ collapse toward $W_U$ itself: the lens has become the plain unembedding projection and inherits its full dimensionality.

So the late rise reports an instrument converging on a trivial limit, not a model spreading its content over more directions.

That cuts both ways. If the shape of this curve at one end is a property of the lens, the flat floor at the other end is a candidate for the same reading — which is the caveat recorded as [[early-layer-lens-degeneracy]].

n-where-it-sits-and-how-little-it-holds.title: The band, the ceiling and the wiring
n-where-it-sits-and-how-little-it-holds.intro: The level above gives the boundaries, the capacity number and the broadcast results. This level gives the instruments that produced them: how the band was first drawn before any of the four statistics were computed, what the sweep at its onset substitutes into the model, what the count of 25 is a count of, and what each broadcast measurement is scored against.

chapters.title: Drawing the boundaries
chapters.body:
The layer numbers need reading first. The paper records 25 evenly spaced layers of the [[residual-stream]] and reindexes them onto a 0 to 100 scale ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). L38 is therefore a point 38 percent of the way through the depth, not the thirty-eighth layer, and the same numbers can be quoted across models of different sizes.

The first cut at the boundaries uses none of the four statistics. For every pair of layers, the paper compares the geometry of the lens vectors by centered kernel alignment: each layer contributes its matrix of pairwise similarities among its own lens vectors, and the two matrices are compared ([[cka]]). The resulting layer-by-layer matrix falls into three blocks — an early block covering roughly the first third, a long middle block, and a small late block ([[fig-27]]).

Blocks alone do not say which block is the workspace. Two anchors settle it, neither of which has to be measured. The final layer's lens vectors must encode next-token predictions, because little else is left for them to encode. The first layer's cannot mean much, because the first layer can only encode the identity of the token sitting at that position. The middle block is what remains, and the three regions take the names [[sensory-layers]], [[workspace-layers]] and [[motor-layers]].

Two hedges travel with the picture. The analyses run on subsampled layers, which makes the block edges look sharper than they are, and in some models the transition is gradual and contains sub-blocks ([[layer-subsampling]]).

The four statistics that refine the boundaries ([[workspace-boundary-metrics]], [[fig-28]]) are all read through the same instrument. So the empty early band may be a failure of the lens at those depths rather than a fact about the model ([[early-layer-lens-degeneracy]]).
chapters.childScope: Take the four boundary statistics one at a time — [[lens-next-token-accuracy]], [[readout-excess-kurtosis]], [[top1-autocorrelation]] against its [[position-shuffled-null]], and [[j-space-effective-dimensionality]] — saying what each quantity measures, why each marks the boundary it marks, and why dimensionality rises a second time at the motor transition as [[jacobian-approaches-identity]] and the readout collapses toward the plain [[unembedding-matrix]] ([[fig-28]]).

chapters.title: One test the lens does not run
chapters.body:
The construction is a substitution at the input. A concept token's input embedding is replaced with the blend $(1-\alpha)\, e_B + \alpha\, e_A$ of two country embeddings, inside ordinary carrier sentences such as "My sister has always wanted to visit ___" ([[embedding-mixture-experiment]]). Sixteen pairs of single-token country names are crossed with forty carrier sentences. For each trial $\alpha$ is swept from 0 to 1, and the residual stream at the mixed token's position is recorded at every layer.

The measurement that follows uses no lens at all. For each trial and each layer, the activation is projected onto the line joining that trial's pure-$B$ activation at $\alpha = 0$ to its pure-$A$ activation at $\alpha = 1$, at the same position and layer. That share is 0 at one end of the sweep and 1 at the other by construction, so the sweep only asks what happens in between. Early layers give a smooth ramp. From about L38 the activation instead sits near one endpoint or the other and jumps between them at a threshold value of $\alpha$ ([[fig-29]]).

The sharpness is then quantified as [[transition-width]]: the change in $\alpha$ needed to move the share from 10 percent to 90 percent. It falls steeply over roughly layers 21 to 42. Measured separately, the activation's component along the two concepts' lens vectors sharpens earlier and further than its complement, which is obtained by projecting the top sixteen lens vectors out ([[j-space-component]], [[fig-70]]).

An average could hide the effect entirely. At the most ambiguous $\alpha$, individual trials do not sit at 0.5: by mid-depth the J-space component's distribution is bimodal near 0 and near 1, while the non-J-space component still carries mass in the middle ([[bimodal-commitment]], [[fig-71]]).

The paper reads this as the analog of [[ignition]]. The input, though, is an embedding blend the model never receives in ordinary text.

chapters.title: What the count of 25 is a count of
chapters.body:
Occupancy is the output of a stopping rule rather than a direct reading. At each position and layer, the paper solves for the sparse nonnegative combination of $K$ lens vectors that best reconstructs the activation ([[sparse-decomposition]]), using gradient pursuit, a greedy sparse-approximation algorithm ([[gradient-pursuit]]). $K$ is raised until the marginal improvement in reconstruction from one more lens vector falls below the improvement offered by a control set of random directions of the same size. The value of $K$ at that crossing is the [[j-space-occupancy]]: near zero through the first third of the layers, and about 25 in the median case across the band, with the value varying by context ([[fig-30]]).

What those vectors account for is separately small. With $K$ set to the median occupancy at each workspace layer, the variance they explain above a same-size random control never exceeds 10 percent ([[excess-variance-explained]]). The activations are dominated by information outside the workspace.

A second decomposition agrees. Only a small share of [[sparse-autoencoder]] features have decoder directions that project sharply through the lens ([[lens-kurtosis]]), and the features that do not are dominated by low-level syntactic and bookkeeping directions ([[bookkeeping-features]]).

One caveat limits what the number means. Occupancy counts lens vectors active above chance, not ideas, and several vectors may stand together for one broader concept ([[vectors-versus-concepts]]).

The formal definition carries the same free parameter. The lens vectors span the whole residual stream, so the J-space is not a subspace at all; fixed at a sparsity level $k$, it is the union of the cones of nonnegative combinations of any $k$ of them ([[eq-jspace-cones]], [[union-of-cones]]). The paper sets $k$ by hand, using values between 10 and 25 for two different purposes ([[sparsity-level-k]]).

chapters.title: Six words at a time, or a whole family
chapters.body:
Presence in the readout is scored by a rule worth stating. The model reads 80-word comma-separated lists, and at each comma a word counts as present if its best rank across the [[workspace-layers]] L38 to L92 falls in the top 25 ([[word-list-experiment]], [[band-min-rank]]). The cutoff is checked rather than assumed: the count of already-read words is plotted against the threshold $K$, alongside control words that never appear in the prompt ([[rank-threshold-robustness]], [[fig-31]]).

Pooling across layers is doing part of the work. Repeating the measurement at the single workspace layer L79 leaves the qualitative picture unchanged but drops the unrelated-word count from about six to one or two ([[single-layer-capacity]], [[fig-72]]). The band holds six because different concepts sit at different depths ([[unrelated-list-capacity]]).

The related-word case is visible from the first item. After the single word "shark", the readout already contains "whale," "fish," "swimming," "submarine," "ocean" — almost none of which have been read ([[category-loading]]).

What clears the workspace is not elapsed time. Eight animals followed by color words leaves the readout dominated by colors after a single color has been presented, and lists built from four consecutive 20-word category blocks show each category entering at its own block and clearing within a few words of the switch ([[category-displacement]]). Within a block, individual words persist long after they are read.

Two further limits sit around the number. The capacity is per token position, and attention can still fetch content from earlier positions ([[per-position-capacity]]). And when the model is told to hold two things at once, two static concepts share tokens at the control rate, 0.46 against 0.53, whereas a concept and a running arithmetic problem almost never share a token, 0.09 against 0.29 ([[workspace-competition]], [[co-occupancy]]).

chapters.title: What the broadcast numbers are compared against
chapters.body:
The claim rests on two directions of travel through the network. Content written into the residual stream at a position is visible to every later layer at that position, and attention makes a position's content available to later positions ([[j-space-broadcast]]).

Depth is measured by gain. For a unit direction $v$ at layer $\ell$, the [[mlp-gain]] is the output norm of the [[mlp-block]] at layer $\ell+1$ applied to $v$, divided by the median output norm over isotropic random directions, so that a random direction scores 1 by construction ([[fig-32]]). The paper flags what the measurement leaves out: the block is applied to the direction on its own, which is never how it is used in practice ([[mlp-gain-context-caveat]]).

The comparison is what carries the result. Sorting sparse autoencoder decoder directions into six equal bins by [[lens-kurtosis]] gives a graded control rather than a binary one, and gain rises monotonically across the bins ([[kappa-strata]]). In the early [[workspace-layers]] the top bin outscores the lens vectors themselves, which the paper takes as evidence that the lens captures only part of the workspace it is estimating.

Across positions the test is on the [[ov-circuit]], the value-then-output map of a head. Gain is one criterion. [[label-preservation]] is the other: the mean reciprocal rank of $\cos(W_{OV} v_i, v_i)$ among that head's cosines with the other directions in the population, referenced to random so that a head copying everything indiscriminately scores zero ([[median-reciprocal-rank]]). Heads are ranked on each criterion, scored by their worse rank, and the best 1 percent are kept ([[broadcast-head-selection-rule]], [[fig-33]]).

The controls are shaped to match. One is the lens vectors under a single fixed random rotation, which preserves their spectrum and pairwise geometry while destroying their alignment with the weights ([[j-rotated-control]]). The selected heads concentrate in the first half of the band, where the lens vectors span the fewest dimensions and one OV map can therefore carry a larger share of them ([[broadcast-head-layer-placement]]).
chapters.childScope: Cover the weight-level broadcast evidence in full: [[neuron-connectivity]] breadth and [[tail-energy]] strength against individual MLP neurons, with the [[read-write-asymmetry]] between early and late workspace layers ([[fig-76]], [[fig-77]], [[fig-78]]); the [[composition-score]] against attention weights and its [[value-vs-query-key-asymmetry]] ([[fig-79]]); and what ablating the [[broadcast-heads]] does and does not disturb, readout recall against behaviour ([[fig-34]]).
